# 5. operator.itemgetter -- lambda se tez (C mein implemented)
from operator import itemgetter
fast = sorted(results, key=itemgetter("duration"))
print([r["name"] for r in fast])

# 6. Objects par attrgetter
from operator import attrgetter
# sorted(test_objects, key=attrgetter("duration"))

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. key=lambda r: r["duration"] — key har element par ek baar call hota hai aur uska result compare hota hai. Original elements ka __lt__ use nahi hota. Isliye dicts sort ho paye (dicts orderable nahi hain!).
    2. reverse=True — sorting ke baad reverse nahi hota, comparison ulta hota hai. Isliye stability preserve rehti hai (sorted(x, reverse=True) aur list(reversed(sorted(x))) ties ke liye alag order dete hain).
    3. key=lambda r: (r["status"], -r["duration"]) — tuple comparison element-wise hoti hai: pehle [0] compare, tie ho toh [1]. -duration se us field ka order ulta ho gaya. Ye trick sirf numbers par kaam karti hai.
    4. Do-pass sort — Timsort stable hai, isliye pehle secondary key se sort karo, phir primary se. Primary sort equal elements ka order nahi bigaadega. Ye technique tab chahiye jab mixed ascending/descending par string fields hon.
    5. itemgetter("duration") — C level callable, lambda se ~20-30% tez. Multiple keys bhi le sakta hai: itemgetter("status", "duration") ek tuple deta hai.
    6. attrgetter("duration") — objects ke liye, lambda o: o.duration ka fast version. Nested bhi chalta hai: attrgetter("result.duration").

    Gotchas¶

    Gotcha 1 — sort() None deta hai.

    names = ["c", "a", "b"]
# names = names.sort()          # names ab None hai!
names.sort()                    # sahi
print(names)                    # ['a', 'b', 'c']

    Gotcha 2 — mixed types sort nahi hote.

    # sorted([1, "a"])              # TypeError: '<' not supported between 'str' and 'int'
print(sorted([1, "a"], key=str))  # [1, 'a']  -- key se sab ko comparable banao

    Python 2 mein ye chalta tha (arbitrary but consistent order) — Python 3 ne ise error banaya kyunki wo order meaningless tha.

    Gotcha 3 — list.remove iterate karte waqt. (2.3 mein dekha, dobara yaad rakho)

    Gotcha 4 — list of lists mein shared inner lists.

    row = [0, 0, 0]
grid = [row, row, row]              # teen naam, ek hi list!
grid[0][0] = 9
print(grid)                         # [[9,0,0],[9,0,0],[9,0,0]]

grid = [[0, 0, 0] for _ in range(3)]   # har baar naya inner list
grid[0][0] = 9
print(grid)                         # [[9,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,0]]

    Gotcha 5 — bade list ka in slow hai.

    import timeit
setup = "data = [f'test_{i}' for i in range(100000)]; target = 'test_99999'"
print(timeit.timeit("target in data", setup=setup, number=1000))          # ~1.0s

setup_set = "data = {f'test_{i}' for i in range(100000)}; target = 'test_99999'"
print(timeit.timeit("target in data", setup=setup_set, number=1000))      # ~0.00005s
    1. List membership O(n) hai — worst case poora scan. Set O(1) average.
    2. Agar aap ek list mein baar-baar in check kar rahe ho, set bana lo: known = set(items). Ek baar O(n) cost, phir har lookup O(1).
    3. Ye QA mein tab dikhta hai jab aap 5000 test IDs ki list mein 5000 baar membership check karte ho — O(n²) = 25 million comparisons.

    Interview answer: "A Python list is a dynamic array of pointers, not a linked list. It keeps two numbers: the number of items and the allocated capacity. append writes into spare capacity in constant time; when capacity runs out CPython reallocates to roughly 1.125 times the new size plus a small constant and copies the pointers, so the occasional O(n) resize is spread over many appends — that's why append is amortised O(1). insert(0, x) and pop(0) are O(n) because every remaining pointer has to be shifted; for a queue I use collections.deque, which is a doubly-linked list of blocks and gives O(1) at both ends. The other complexity facts I keep in mind are that membership on a list is O(n) — so if I'm checking repeatedly I build a set once — and that sorting is Timsort: O(n log n), stable, and linear on already-sorted data. Stability is what lets me sort by name and then by status to get a two-level ordering."

    Cross-question — "Why does CPython over-allocate by only ~12.5% rather than doubling, like C++ vector?" "It's a memory-versus-copies trade-off, and CPython chose memory. Doubling gives fewer reallocations but wastes up to 50 percent of the allocation; growing by an eighth wastes far less, which matters because a typical Python process holds a very large number of small lists. The amortised cost is still O(1) either way — any geometric growth factor greater than 1 gives amortised constant time; the factor only changes the constant. CPython also adds a fixed term so tiny lists don't reallocate on every single append, and rounds the capacity to a multiple of 4 for allocator friendliness. And if you know the final size, list(range(n)) or a comprehension is faster than repeated appends because CPython can pre-size the array from the iterable's __length_hint__."

    3.2 Tuples — immutable sequences aur unka asli maqsad¶

    Kya hai¶

    Tuple ek immutable sequence hai. Ek baar bana, uske slots nahi badal sakte.

    Analogy: list ek shopping bag hai (cheezein daalo-nikalo). Tuple ek sealed courier packet hai — andar kya hai wo fix hai. Packet ke andar agar ek khula dabba (list) ho toh us dabbe ka saamaan badal sakta hai, par packet mein kaunsa dabba hai wo nahi.

    Kyu hai — sirf "immutable list" nahi¶

    Log kehte hain "tuple = immutable list". Ye galat framing hai. Asli farak semantic hai:

    List Tuple
    Semantics homogeneous — same kism ki cheezein, variable count heterogeneous — ek record ke alag-alag fields
    Mental model "test names ki list" "(name, status, duration) ek test ka record"
    Position ka matlab koi nahi (order bas order hai) har position ka alag matlab hai
    Hashable Nahi Haan (agar elements hashable)
    Memory zyada (spare capacity) kam (exact)

    Isliye ("test_login", "passed", 1.2) tuple hai, aur ["test_a", "test_b", "test_c"] list.

    Practical reasons — chaar concrete faayde¶

    1. Dict key ban sakta hai

    # Test result cache: (test_name, browser, env) -> result
cache = {}
cache[("test_login", "chromium", "staging")] = "passed"
cache[("test_login", "firefox", "staging")] = "failed"

print(cache[("test_login", "chromium", "staging")])     # passed

# List key se error:
# cache[["test_login", "chromium"]] = "x"     # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
    1. cache[("test_login", "chromium", "staging")] — composite key. Ye ek nested dict (cache["test_login"]["chromium"]["staging"]) se saaf hai jab teeno dimensions hamesha saath aate hain.
    2. Tuple hashable hai kyunki wo immutable hai → uska hash lifetime bhar constant rahega → dict apna entry dobara dhoondh sakta hai. List mutable hai, toh agar wo key hoti aur badal jaati toh dict ka bucket galat ho jaata aur entry "kho" jaati. Isliye Python list ko hashable hi nahi banata.

    2. Multiple return values

    def run_test(name):
    # ... test chalao ...
    return name, "passed", 1.23                # ye ek TUPLE hai (brackets optional)

name, status, duration = run_test("test_login")   # unpacking
print(status)                                      # passed

result = run_test("test_cart")                     # tuple as a whole
print(result[1])                                   # passed  (par ye readable nahi hai)
    1. return name, "passed", 1.23 — comma se tuple banti hai, brackets se nahi. (1) ek int hai, (1,) ek tuple. Ye Python ki sabse common syntax galti hai.
    2. name, status, duration = ... — tuple unpacking. Count exactly match hona chahiye warna ValueError: too many values to unpack.
    3. result[1] — magic index. 3+ fields ho toh NamedTuple ya dataclass use karo (3.6, 5.11).

    3. Unpacking / swapping

    a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a                       # swap -- temp variable ki zarurat nahi
print(a, b)                       # 2 1

first, *middle, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]      # starred unpacking
print(first, middle, last)                  # 1 [2, 3, 4] 5

(name, (status, duration)) = ("test_a", ("passed", 1.2))   # nested unpacking
print(name, status, duration)               # test_a passed 1.2

first, _, third = (1, 2, 3)                 # '_' = "mujhe ye nahi chahiye"
print(first, third)                         # 1 3
    1. a, b = b, a — right side pehle poora evaluate hoke ek tuple (2, 1) banta hai, phir unpack hota hai. Isliye temp variable nahi chahiye. C mein ye nahi ho sakta.
    2. first, *middle, last = [...] — *middle list deta hai (tuple nahi), aur exactly ek star allowed hai. Ye "pehla aur aakhri chahiye, beech ka chahe jitna ho" ke liye perfect hai.
    3. Nested unpacking structure ko match karta hai.
    4. _ ek normal naam hai (convention se "ignored"), aur linters isko unused nahi maante. Multiple ignores ke liye _ reuse kar sakte ho ya __, ___ use kar sakte ho.

    4. Memory aur speed

    import sys, timeit

print(sys.getsizeof([1, 2, 3]))       # 88   -- list mein spare capacity ka overhead
print(sys.getsizeof((1, 2, 3)))       # 64   -- tuple exact size

print(timeit.timeit("(1, 2, 3)", number=1_000_000))       # ~0.01s -- constant, folded
print(timeit.timeit("[1, 2, 3]", number=1_000_000))       # ~0.05s -- har baar naya object
    1. Tuple chhota hai kyunki usme allocated field ki zarurat nahi — size fix hai.
    2. (1, 2, 3) constant folding se compile time par hi ban jaata hai aur co_consts mein store hota hai — runtime par sirf LOAD_CONST. [1, 2, 3] har baar BUILD_LIST karta hai kyunki list mutable hai aur usko share nahi kiya ja sakta.
    3. CPython chhote tuples ka free list bhi rakhta hai (reuse), toh allocation bhi sasta hai.

    Tuple ke methods — sirf do¶

    t = ("passed", "failed", "passed")
print(t.count("passed"))          # 2   -- O(n)
print(t.index("failed"))          # 1   -- O(n), not found par ValueError
print(len(t))                     # 3   -- O(1)
print("passed" in t)              # True -- O(n)
print(t + ("skipped",))           # naya tuple -- O(n+k)
print(t * 2)                      # naya tuple, repeat
print(t[::-1])                    # ('passed', 'failed', 'passed') reversed slice

    Sirf count aur index hain kyunki baaki sab methods mutate karte — tuple pe unka matlab hi nahi.

    Gotchas¶

    Gotcha 1 — single-element tuple ke liye comma zaruri hai.

    not_a_tuple = ("test_login")           # ye bas ek STRING hai, brackets grouping ke liye
print(type(not_a_tuple))               # <class 'str'>
print(len(not_a_tuple))                # 10  -- string ki length!

a_tuple = ("test_login",)              # comma se tuple
print(type(a_tuple), len(a_tuple))     # <class 'tuple'> 1

also_tuple = "test_login",             # brackets ki zarurat hi nahi
print(type(also_tuple))                # <class 'tuple'>
    1. Comma tuple banata hai, brackets nahi. Brackets sirf precedence/grouping ke liye hain.
    2. Ye bug real hai: @pytest.mark.parametrize("x", ("a")) chalega par har character alag test ban jaayega ("a" iterate hoke 'a'), aur ("a",) ek test dega. Aur function call mein f(x) vs f((x,)) ka farak.
    3. Empty tuple ke liye () kaafi hai — koi ambiguity nahi.

    Gotcha 2 — immutable ka matlab "andar ka bhi immutable" nahi.

    config = ("staging", ["chromium", "firefox"])
config[1].append("webkit")                 # list mutate ho gayi -- LEGAL
print(config)                              # ('staging', ['chromium', 'firefox', 'webkit'])

# config[0] = "prod"                       # TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

# print(hash(config))                      # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
    1. Tuple ke slots fix hain — config[0] = ... fail hoga.
    2. Par slot mein jo object hai wo agar mutable hai toh wo badal sakta hai.
    3. Aur isi wajah se ye tuple hashable nahi hai — kyunki hash(tuple) apne elements ke hashes ko combine karta hai, aur list ka hash hai hi nahi. Ye ek achha proof hai ki "hashable = deep immutability" hai, "shallow immutability" nahi.
    4. Poori immutability chahiye toh ("staging", ("chromium", "firefox")).

    Gotcha 3 — trailing comma se accidental tuple.

    timeout = 30,                              # <- galti se comma
print(timeout)                             # (30,)
# print(timeout * 2)                       # (30, 30)  -- 60 nahi!

    Ye copy-paste karte waqt hota hai aur error message door milta hai.

    Gotcha 4 — += tuple par naya object banata hai.

    t = (1, 2)
t2 = t
t += (3,)
print(t, t2)                               # (1, 2, 3) (1, 2)   -- t2 nahi badla

    Kyunki tuple mein __iadd__ nahi hai, fallback t = t + (3,) par hota hai. Loop mein ye quadratic hai — list mein collect karo phir tuple() kar lo.

    Interview answer: "The textbook answer is that a tuple is an immutable list, but that's the wrong framing. The real distinction is semantic: a list is a homogeneous collection of variable length where the position carries no meaning, while a tuple is a heterogeneous record where each position means something specific — (name, status, duration). That's why tuples are what functions return for multiple values and what unpacking works on. Practically, immutability buys three things: tuples are hashable so they work as dict keys and set members — I use (test_name, browser, env) as a cache key rather than a triple-nested dict — they're smaller and constant-folded by the compiler, and they're safe to share. The two traps are that a single-element tuple needs the trailing comma, since it's the comma and not the parentheses that makes a tuple, and that immutability is shallow: ('env', ['a']) lets you append to the inner list, and that same tuple is unhashable because hashing recurses into the elements."

    Cross-question — "If tuples are immutable, why does hash(('a', [])) fail rather than just hashing the identity of the list?" "Because hashing has a contract: objects that compare equal must hash equal, and an object's hash must not change while it's in a hash table. tuple.__hash__ combines the hashes of its elements, so equal tuples hash equal. If it fell back to the list's identity, two tuples that compare equal — ('a', [1]) and ('a', [1]) with different list objects — would hash differently, which silently breaks dict and set lookups. Python's answer is to refuse: list.__hash__ is None, so the recursive hash raises TypeError immediately rather than letting you build a container that misbehaves later."

    3.3 Sets and frozensets¶

    Kya hai¶

    set ek unordered collection of unique hashable objects hai. Internally wo ek hash table hai jismein sirf keys hain, values nahi.

    Analogy: ek guest list jahan har naam sirf ek baar likha ja sakta hai, aur order matter nahi karta — sirf "ye naam hai ya nahi" matter karta hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    # --- WITHOUT set: dedup karna O(n^2) ---
all_tags = ["smoke", "auth", "smoke", "regression", "auth"]
unique = []
for tag in all_tags:
    if tag not in unique:              # O(n) scan har item ke liye -> O(n^2) total
        unique.append(tag)
print(unique)                          # ['smoke', 'auth', 'regression']

# --- WITH set: O(n) ---
unique = list(set(all_tags))           # O(n), par ORDER kho gaya
print(unique)                          # ['auth', 'smoke', 'regression'] -- random order

# --- Order preserve karke dedup: dict.fromkeys (3.7+) ---
unique = list(dict.fromkeys(all_tags))  # O(n) AUR order preserved
print(unique)                           # ['smoke', 'auth', 'regression']

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. if tag not in unique: — list par in O(n) hai, aur ye har item ke liye chalta hai → O(n²). 10,000 tags par 50 million comparisons.
    2. set(all_tags) — har element ka hash compute hota hai aur hash table mein daala jaata hai. Duplicate ka hash same hoga aur == bhi, toh wo skip ho jaayega. Total O(n).
    3. list(set(...)) — set ka iteration order hash order hai, insertion order nahi. Aur strings ka hash PYTHONHASHSEED se randomise hota hai (security feature), toh har run mein order alag ho sakta hai. Isliye test assertions mein kabhi list(set(...)) ka order assume mat karo — sorted(set(...)) likho.
    4. dict.fromkeys(all_tags) — dict banata hai jismein keys wahi hain aur values None. Python 3.7+ mein dict insertion-ordered hai, toh order preserve rehta hai. Ye "ordered dedup" ka standard idiom hai.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Set ek open-addressed hash table hai:

    hash("smoke") = 8398279183...
index = hash & (table_size - 1)      # bitmask -- table size hamesha 2 ki power hai
slot 5: "smoke"

hash("auth")  = 1928374...
index = 3
slot 3: "auth"

Collision hui? -> probe sequence follow karo (open addressing, perturbation ke saath)

    Do cheezein zaruri:

    1. __hash__ — object se ek int. Hashable hona chahiye.
    2. __eq__ — collision ke baad confirm karne ke liye ki wahi object hai.

    Contract: a == b ho toh hash(a) == hash(b) hona hi chahiye. Ulta zaruri nahi (collision allowed hai).

    Load factor 3/5 se zyada hone par table resize hoti hai (double ya zyada) aur saare elements dobara insert hote hain — isliye add amortised O(1) hai.

    Saare set operations¶

    smoke = {"test_login", "test_cart", "test_home"}
regression = {"test_cart", "test_pay", "test_refund"}

# --- MEMBERSHIP (O(1) average) ---
print("test_cart" in smoke)                # True
print("test_xyz" not in smoke)             # True

# --- ADD / REMOVE ---
s = set()                                  # KHAALI SET aise banao -- {} khaali DICT hai!
s.add("test_a")                            # O(1) -- ek item
s.update(["test_b", "test_c"])             # O(k) -- multiple items
s.discard("test_zzz")                      # O(1) -- na ho toh CHUP RAHO
s.remove("test_a")                         # O(1) -- na ho toh KeyError
popped = s.pop()                           # O(1) -- ARBITRARY element nikaalta hai
s.clear()                                  # O(n)

# --- SET ALGEBRA (operator aur method dono) ---
print(smoke | regression)                  # union         {sab}
print(smoke.union(regression))             # same, par ye kisi bhi iterable ko leta hai

print(smoke & regression)                  # intersection  {'test_cart'}
print(smoke.intersection(regression))

print(smoke - regression)                  # difference    {'test_login', 'test_home'}
print(smoke.difference(regression))

print(smoke ^ regression)                  # symmetric diff -- sirf ek mein hain
print(smoke.symmetric_difference(regression))

# --- IN-PLACE versions ---
a = {1, 2}
a |= {3}                                   # a.update({3})
a &= {2, 3}                                # a.intersection_update({2, 3})
a -= {3}                                   # a.difference_update({3})
a ^= {2, 9}                                # a.symmetric_difference_update({2, 9})
print(a)

# --- RELATIONSHIPS ---
print({"test_cart"} <= smoke)              # True  -- subset
print({"test_cart"} < smoke)               # True  -- PROPER subset (aur equal nahi)
print(smoke >= {"test_cart"})              # True  -- superset
print(smoke.isdisjoint({"test_zzz"}))      # True  -- koi common element nahi
print(smoke == {"test_home", "test_cart", "test_login"})   # True -- order matter nahi karta

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. s = set() — {} khaali dict banata hai, khaali set nahi. Ye historical hai: dict pehle aaya tha. Khaali set ke liye set() hi likhna padta hai. Non-empty set ke liye {1, 2} theek hai.
    2. s.discard(x) vs s.remove(x) — discard missing par chup rehta hai, remove KeyError deta hai. Choice deliberate karo: agar aapko pata hona chahiye ki item tha ya nahi, remove use karo. Warna discard — warna aapko try/except KeyError: pass likhna padega jo Part 9 ka anti-pattern hai.
    3. s.pop() — arbitrary element hatata hai, "aakhri" nahi (set mein aakhri hota hi nahi). Deterministic behaviour chahiye toh min(s) ya sorted(s)[0] use karo.
    4. smoke | regression vs smoke.union(regression) — operator dono taraf set maangta hai; method koi bhi iterable le leta hai: smoke.union(["a", "b"]) chalega par smoke | ["a", "b"] TypeError dega. Ye chhota sa farak API design mein kaam aata hai.
    5. smoke ^ regression — symmetric difference. QA ka killer use case: do test runs compare karo — run1_passed ^ run2_passed woh tests deta hai jinka status badla (flaky candidates).
    6. {"test_cart"} <= smoke — subset. < proper subset hai (subset aur equal nahi). <= issubset() ka operator form hai.
    7. smoke.isdisjoint(other) — ye not (smoke & other) se tez hai kyunki wo intersection set banaye bina short-circuit karta hai — pehla common element milte hi False.
    8. smoke == {...} — set equality order-independent hai. Test assertions ke liye perfect: assert set(actual_ids) == set(expected_ids) order-agnostic comparison deta hai.

    frozenset — immutable set¶

    BROWSERS = frozenset({"chromium", "firefox", "webkit"})     # constant, koi galti se badal na de

# frozenset hashable hai -> set ke andar set daal sakte ho
test_groups = {
    frozenset({"test_login", "test_logout"}),
    frozenset({"test_cart", "test_pay"}),
}
print(len(test_groups))                    # 2

# ya dict key ke roop mein
coverage = {
    frozenset({"chromium", "firefox"}): "cross-browser",
    frozenset({"chromium"}): "single",
}
print(coverage[frozenset({"firefox", "chromium"})])    # 'cross-browser' -- order matter nahi
    1. frozenset ke paas saare read operations hain (|, &, -, in, issubset) par koi mutating method nahi (add, remove, update nahi).
    2. Hashable hone se wo set ka element ya dict ki key ban sakta hai — jo tab chahiye jab aapko "set of sets" ya "unordered combination as key" chahiye.
    3. coverage[frozenset({"firefox", "chromium"})] — order alag hai par frozenset ka hash order par depend nahi karta, toh lookup kaam karta hai. Ye ek genuinely useful pattern hai: "kaunse browsers ke combination par ye test chalta hai".

    QA use cases — set algebra se real problems¶

    expected = {"test_login", "test_cart", "test_pay", "test_search"}
collected = {"test_login", "test_cart", "test_new_feature"}

missing = expected - collected               # jo chalne chahiye the par collect nahi hue
extra = collected - expected                 # naye tests jo baseline mein nahi hain
common = expected & collected                # dono mein
changed = expected ^ collected               # kisi ek mein

print(f"missing ({len(missing)}): {sorted(missing)}")
print(f"extra   ({len(extra)}): {sorted(extra)}")

# Flaky detection: do runs mein status compare
run1_passed = {"test_a", "test_b", "test_c"}
run2_passed = {"test_a", "test_c", "test_d"}
flaky = run1_passed ^ run2_passed             # jinka result badla
print(f"flaky candidates: {sorted(flaky)}")   # ['test_b', 'test_d']
    1. expected - collected — "missing" ka seedha, padhne layak expression. Loop se likhne mein 6 lines lagti aur bug ka chance hota.
    2. sorted(missing) — hamesha print/assert karte waqt sort karo, warna output har run mein alag order mein aayega aur diff karna mushkil hoga.
    3. run1_passed ^ run2_passed — flaky detection ek line mein. Ye asli production-grade idiom hai.

    Gotchas¶

    Gotcha 1 — set unordered hai aur order run-to-run badal sakta hai.

    print(list({"b", "a", "c"}))       # order unpredictable, aur PYTHONHASHSEED se run-to-run badalta
    1. Python 3.3+ mein string hashing randomised hai (hash-collision DoS attack se bachne ke liye). Isliye set/dict-of-strings ka iteration order har process mein alag ho sakta hai.
    2. PYTHONHASHSEED=0 set karke ise disable kar sakte ho — CI debugging ke liye kabhi-kabhi useful hai, par production mein nahi.
    3. Test assertion mein kabhi set ka order use mat karo. sorted() lagao.

    Gotcha 2 — set ke elements hashable hone chahiye.

    # s = {[1, 2]}          # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
s = {(1, 2)}            # tuple chalega
s = {frozenset([1, 2])} # frozenset chalega

    Gotcha 3 — 1, True, 1.0 ek hi element hain.

    print({1, True, 1.0, "1"})       # {1, '1'}   -- teen numbers collapse ho gaye

    Kyunki 1 == True == 1.0 aur unke hash same hain (1.3 wala rule).

    Gotcha 4 — set comprehension aur khaali braces.

    empty_dict = {}
empty_set = set()
print(type(empty_dict), type(empty_set))     # <class 'dict'> <class 'set'>

nonempty_set = {x for x in range(3)}         # set comprehension
empty_from_comp = {x for x in []}            # ye SET hai (khaali), dict nahi
print(type(empty_from_comp))                 # <class 'set'>

    Gotcha 5 — mutable object ko set mein daalne ke baad mutate karna.

    class Test:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(self.name)           # hash MUTABLE field par based hai -- KHATRA
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Test) and self.name == other.name

t = Test("test_a")
s = {t}
print(t in s)                            # True
t.name = "test_b"                        # hash badal gaya!
print(t in s)                            # False   <- apna hi object nahi mil raha
print(len(s))                            # 1       <- par set mein hai
    1. __hash__ mutable field par based hai. Object set mein us bucket mein para hai jo purane hash se nikla tha. Naam badalne ke baad lookup naye hash se hota hai → galat bucket → not found.
    2. Rule: __hash__ sirf immutable fields par based hona chahiye — ideally ek ID jo kabhi na badle. Ya class ko frozen banao (@dataclass(frozen=True)).

    Interview answer: "A set is a hash table with keys and no values, so membership, add, and discard are O(1) on average rather than the O(n) you get scanning a list. Two things follow from that: elements must be hashable, and iteration order is hash order, not insertion order — and since Python 3.3 string hashing is randomised per process, so that order can differ between runs. That means never asserting on the order of a set; I sort it first. The operations I actually reach for in QA are set algebra: expected - collected gives me the tests that didn't get collected, and run1_passed ^ run2_passed gives the symmetric difference between two runs, which is exactly my flaky-test candidate list — both in one readable line. frozenset is the immutable version, and it's hashable, so I use it when I need a set of sets or an order-independent composite dict key. One trap worth mentioning: {} is an empty dict, not an empty set — you need set()."

    Cross-question — "How does a set handle hash collisions?" "CPython uses open addressing with a perturbation-based probe sequence, not chaining. When the computed slot is taken it probes another slot using a recurrence that mixes in the remaining high bits of the hash, so probe sequences for different keys diverge quickly and clustering stays low. Each slot stores the full hash alongside the key, so a probe can reject a non-match on the cheap integer comparison and only calls __eq__ when the hashes match. The table is kept below about a 3/5 load factor; crossing that triggers a resize to a power of two and a full reinsert, which is what makes add amortised O(1). Worst case is still O(n) if every key collides — which is exactly the denial-of-service attack that hash randomisation was introduced to prevent."

    3.4 Dicts — hashing, collisions, aur insertion order¶

    Kya hai¶

    dict ek hash map hai: key → value. Python ka sabse important data structure hai — kyunki namespaces, objects ke attributes, keyword arguments, JSON, aur modules sab dicts hi hain.

    Analogy: ek library catalogue. Book ka title (key) se aap turant shelf number (value) nikal lete ho — poori library scan nahi karni padti. Catalogue ka index title ke pehle akshar se banta hai (hash), aur do books ka pehla akshar same ho toh aap us section mein thoda dhoondhte ho (collision resolution).

    Kaise kaam karta hai — compact dict (3.6+)¶

    Python 3.6 se pehle dict aisa tha:

    PURANA (3.5 aur pehle) -- sparse table, har slot mein poora entry
+----+---------------------------+
| 0  | (empty)                   |
| 1  | hash, key, value          |   <- 24 bytes har slot, chahe khaali ho
| 2  | (empty)                   |
| 3  | (empty)                   |
| 4  | hash, key, value          |
| 5  | (empty)                   |
| 6  | (empty)                   |
| 7  | (empty)                   |
+----+---------------------------+
Memory waste: 6 khaali slots x 24 bytes = 144 bytes bekaar
Order: hash order, insertion order NAHI

    3.6 se compact dict:

    NAYA -- do structures

indices (chhota array, sirf int):        entries (dense array, sirf bhare hue)
+----+------+                            +---+------------+----------+---------+
| 0  |  -1  |  (empty)                   | 0 | hash_a     | "env"    | "stag"  |
| 1  |   0  |  -> entries[0]             | 1 | hash_b     | "browser"| "chrom" |
| 2  |  -1  |                            | 2 | hash_c     | "retry"  | 2       |
| 3  |   2  |  -> entries[2]             +---+------------+----------+---------+
| 4  |  -1  |                                  ^ INSERTION ORDER mein
| 5  |   1  |  -> entries[1]
| 6  |  -1  |
| 7  |  -1  |
+----+------+
Memory: indices array mein sirf ek int per slot (1/2/4/8 bytes, size ke hisaab se)
Order: entries array insertion order mein hai -> iteration insertion-ordered!

    Do faayde ek saath:

    1. Memory ~30-35% kam — sparse array mein ab sirf small ints hain, poore 24-byte entries nahi.
    2. Insertion order preserve — ye ek side effect tha, design goal nahi. 3.6 mein ye "implementation detail" tha; 3.7 mein language spec ka hissa ban gaya aur ab guaranteed hai.

    Lookup ka poora flow¶

    d = {"env": "staging", "browser": "chromium"}
value = d["browser"]

    Steps:

    1. hash("browser") compute hota hai (string ka hash cached hota hai str object mein, toh doosri baar free hai).
    2. index = hash & (table_size - 1) — mask se slot nikalta hai. Table size hamesha 2 ki power hai, isliye modulo ki jagah bitmask — bahut tez.
    3. indices[index] se entries ka position milta hai.
    4. entries[pos].hash == hash check — agar nahi, collision hai → probe next slot.
    5. Hash match hua toh entries[pos].key == key (__eq__) check — kyunki alag keys ka hash same ho sakta hai.
    6. Match → value return.

    Average O(1). Worst case O(n) (sab keys collide karein).

    Dict ke saare operations¶

    config = {"env": "staging", "browser": "chromium", "retries": 2}

# --- READ ---
print(config["env"])                        # O(1), missing key par KeyError
print(config.get("timeout"))                # O(1), missing par None
print(config.get("timeout", 30))            # O(1), missing par 30
print(config.setdefault("timeout", 30))     # get + agar missing ho toh SET bhi karo
print("env" in config)                      # O(1) -- KEYS mein dekhta hai
print(30 in config.values())                # O(n) -- values mein linear scan

# --- WRITE ---
config["headless"] = True                   # O(1) amortised
config.update({"retries": 3, "slowmo": 100})# O(k)
config.update(retries=5)                    # kwargs form
config |= {"trace": "on"}                   # Python 3.9+ in-place merge
merged = config | {"video": "on"}           # Python 3.9+ NAYA dict

# --- DELETE ---
del config["slowmo"]                        # O(1), missing par KeyError
removed = config.pop("trace")               # O(1), value return karta hai
safe = config.pop("nonexistent", None)      # default se KeyError se bacho
last_item = config.popitem()                # O(1), AAKHRI (LIFO) pair nikaalta hai (3.7+)
config.clear()                              # O(n)

# --- VIEWS (lazy, live) ---
config = {"env": "staging", "browser": "chromium"}
print(list(config.keys()))                  # ['env', 'browser']
print(list(config.values()))                # ['staging', 'chromium']
print(list(config.items()))                 # [('env', 'staging'), ('browser', 'chromium')]

# --- CONSTRUCTION ---
d1 = dict(env="staging", browser="chromium")            # kwargs (keys valid identifiers honi chahiye)
d2 = dict([("env", "staging"), ("browser", "chrome")])  # pairs se
d3 = dict.fromkeys(["a", "b", "c"], 0)                  # sab keys, ek hi default value
d4 = {k: v for k, v in d1.items() if v}                 # comprehension
print(d3)                                                # {'a': 0, 'b': 0, 'c': 0}

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. config["env"] vs config.get("env") — pehla missing par KeyError uthata hai, doosra None deta hai. Choice deliberate karo: agar key ka hona mandatory hai toh [] likho — crash aapko batayega ki config galat hai. Agar optional hai toh .get(). Har jagah .get() likhna galtiyaan chhupata hai.
    2. config.setdefault("timeout", 30) — agar key hai toh uski value do, warna set karke wo do. Ek call mein "get or create". Grouping ke liye ye idiom hai: 
      groups = {}
for r in results:
    groups.setdefault(r["status"], []).append(r["name"])
      Caveat: default value hamesha evaluate hoti hai, chahe key ho ya na ho. Agar default costly ho (setdefault(k, expensive())) toh wo har baar chalega — tab defaultdict ya explicit if better hai.
    3. 30 in config.values() — O(n), kyunki values hash-indexed nahi hain. Agar aapko values se lookup chahiye toh reverse dict banao.
    4. config |= {...} (3.9+) — in-place merge, update() ke barabar. config | {...} naya dict deta hai. Ye {**a, **b} ka readable version hai.
    5. config.pop("nonexistent", None) — default hone se KeyError nahi aata. Ye try/except KeyError se saaf hai.
    6. config.popitem() — 3.7+ mein LIFO (aakhri insert hua pair). Pehle arbitrary tha. Iska use case: dict ko stack ki tarah drain karna.
    7. .keys(), .values(), .items() — ye views hain, lists nahi. Views live hain: dict badle toh view bhi badalta hai. Aur keys() aur items() set-like hain, toh unpar set operations chalti hain: 
      a = {"x": 1, "y": 2}
b = {"y": 2, "z": 3}
print(a.keys() & b.keys())      # {'y'}  -- common keys
print(a.items() & b.items())    # {('y', 2)}  -- common key-value pairs
print(a.keys() - b.keys())      # {'x'}
      values() set-like nahi hai (values hashable nahi ho sakti aur duplicate ho sakti hain).
    8. dict(env="staging") — kwargs form. Limitation: keys valid Python identifiers honi chahiye. dict(content-type="x") SyntaxError hai — us case mein {"content-type": "x"} likhna padega.
    9. dict.fromkeys(["a","b"], 0) — saavdhaan: agar default mutable ho toh saari keys ek hi object share karengi! 
      d = dict.fromkeys(["a", "b"], [])       # KHATRA
d["a"].append(1)
print(d)                                # {'a': [1], 'b': [1]}   <- dono badal gaye
      Ye 1.4 wala mutable-default bug hai, dict ke roop mein.

    Merging — teen tareeke¶

    base = {"env": "staging", "timeout": 30}
override = {"timeout": 60, "headless": True}

# 1. Python 3.9+ -- sabse saaf
merged = base | override
print(merged)                # {'env': 'staging', 'timeout': 60, 'headless': True}

# 2. Unpacking (3.5+) -- 3.9 se pehle ka standard
merged = {**base, **override}

# 3. copy + update -- purana
merged = base.copy()
merged.update(override)
    1. Teeno mein right wins — override ka timeout jeeta.
    2. Teeno shallow hain — nested dicts share hote hain. Nested override chahiye toh recursive merge khud likhna padega: 
      def deep_merge(base, override):
    out = dict(base)                                    # shallow copy top level
    for k, v in override.items():
        if isinstance(v, dict) and isinstance(out.get(k), dict):
            out[k] = deep_merge(out[k], v)              # dono dict hain -> recurse
        else:
            out[k] = v                                  # warna replace
    return out
      Ye pytest config, Playwright config, ya environment-specific overrides ke liye exactly wahi hai jo chahiye.

    Insertion order — kya guarantee hai¶

    d = {}
d["z"] = 1
d["a"] = 2
d["m"] = 3
print(list(d))                  # ['z', 'a', 'm']   -- INSERTION order, sorted nahi

d["z"] = 99                     # existing key UPDATE -- position nahi badalti
print(list(d))                  # ['z', 'a', 'm']

del d["z"]
d["z"] = 100                    # delete + re-insert -- ab AAKHIR mein
print(list(d))                  # ['a', 'm', 'z']
    1. Update position nahi badalta, sirf value badalti hai — kyunki entry apni jagah par hi overwrite hoti hai.
    2. Delete + insert position badalta hai — delete se entry mein tombstone lagta hai, aur naya insert entries array ke end mein jaata hai.
    3. == order-independent hai: {"a":1,"b":2} == {"b":2,"a":1} True hai. Order sirf iteration ke liye hai. Agar aapko order-sensitive comparison chahiye toh list(d1.items()) == list(d2.items()).

    Dict comprehension examples (QA-flavoured)¶

    results = [
    {"name": "test_login", "status": "passed", "duration": 1.2},
    {"name": "test_cart", "status": "failed", "duration": 4.5},
    {"name": "test_pay", "status": "failed", "duration": 0.8},
]

# 1. name -> duration lookup
durations = {r["name"]: r["duration"] for r in results}

# 2. Filter karke
slow = {r["name"]: r["duration"] for r in results if r["duration"] > 1.0}

# 3. Value transform
ms = {name: int(sec * 1000) for name, sec in durations.items()}
print(ms)                    # {'test_login': 1200, 'test_cart': 4500, 'test_pay': 800}

# 4. Key normalise (case-insensitive headers)
raw_headers = {"Content-Type": "json", "X-Request-ID": "abc"}
normalised = {k.lower(): v for k, v in raw_headers.items()}
print(normalised)            # {'content-type': 'json', 'x-request-id': 'abc'}

# 5. Invert (values unique honi chahiye!)
inverted = {v: k for k, v in durations.items()}

# 6. Grouping -- comprehension se NAHI ho sakta cleanly, loop use karo
from collections import defaultdict
by_status = defaultdict(list)
for r in results:
    by_status[r["status"]].append(r["name"])
print(dict(by_status))       # {'passed': ['test_login'], 'failed': ['test_cart', 'test_pay']}

    Gotchas¶

    Gotcha 1 — iterate karte hue dict modify karna.

    config = {"a": 1, "b": None, "c": 3}
# for k in config:
#     if config[k] is None:
#         del config[k]          # RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration

# Fix 1: keys ki snapshot lo
for k in list(config):             # list() ek copy banata hai
    if config[k] is None:
        del config[k]
print(config)                      # {'a': 1, 'c': 3}

# Fix 2 (behtar): naya dict banao
config = {"a": 1, "b": None, "c": 3}
config = {k: v for k, v in config.items() if v is not None}
print(config)
    1. Dict ka iterator ek version counter rakhta hai. Size badle toh wo turant RuntimeError deta hai — list se behtar behaviour, kyunki silent skip nahi hota.
    2. Note: value badalna (config[k] = 0) allowed hai — sirf size badalna nahi.
    3. list(config) keys ki list banata hai — list(config.keys()) ka short form.

    Gotcha 2 — unhashable key.

    # d = {[1, 2]: "x"}         # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
d = {(1, 2): "x"}           # tuple chalega

    Gotcha 3 — dict.get ka default hamesha evaluate hota hai.

    def expensive_default():
    print("computing default...")
    return 42

d = {"a": 1}
print(d.get("a", expensive_default()))    # "computing default..." PRINT HOGA, phir 1
    1. Python eager hai — arguments call se pehle evaluate hote hain. get ko jo default mila wo already computed value hai.
    2. Fix: d["a"] if "a" in d else expensive_default() — ye lazy hai (conditional expression short-circuit karti hai). Ya defaultdict (3.6) jo factory ko sirf zarurat par call karta hai.

    Gotcha 4 — dict ordering par assert karna cross-version.

    # 3.7+ par safe:
assert list(d.keys()) == ["a", "b"]
# 3.6 par "implementation detail" tha, 3.5 par bilkul galat.
# JSON round-trip ke baad order preserve hota hai (json module order maintain karta hai)

    Gotcha 5 — keys() view live hai.

    d = {"a": 1}
ks = d.keys()
d["b"] = 2
print(list(ks))          # ['a', 'b']   <- view khud update ho gaya!

    Agar snapshot chahiye toh list(d.keys()) ek baar hi kar lo.

    Interview answer: "A dict is a hash table, and since 3.6 CPython uses a compact layout: a small array of integer indices plus a dense array of entries in insertion order. That cut memory by around a third, and insertion-ordered iteration fell out of it as a side effect — which was an implementation detail in 3.6 and became a language guarantee in 3.7. Lookup hashes the key, masks it to a slot, follows the index into the entries array, compares the cached hash first and only then calls __eq__, so it's O(1) average and O(n) worst case if everything collides. Practically: d[k] versus d.get(k) is a real design decision — I use the bracket form when a missing key means the config is wrong and I want the crash, and get only when absent is genuinely valid. keys() and items() are set-like views, so a.keys() & b.keys() gives me common keys without building lists. And you can't add or remove keys while iterating — Python raises RuntimeError rather than silently skipping, which is friendlier than list's behaviour."

    Cross-question — "You said dicts are ordered now. Does that make OrderedDict obsolete?" "Mostly, but not entirely. OrderedDict still has three things a plain dict doesn't: its __eq__ is order-sensitive, so OrderedDict([('a',1),('b',2)]) != OrderedDict([('b',2),('a',1)]) while the plain dicts compare equal; it has move_to_end(key, last=True/False), which is what you build an LRU cache with; and its popitem(last=False) can pop from the front, giving you FIFO, whereas dict's popitem is LIFO only. So if order is part of the value's identity, or you need to reorder in place, OrderedDict is still the right type. For everything else — which is almost everything — a plain dict is smaller and faster."

    3.5 Strings as immutable sequences — aur += loop ka quadratic jaal¶

    Kya hai¶

    str ek immutable sequence of Unicode code points hai. "Sequence" matlab indexable, sliceable, iterable, len()-able. "Immutable" matlab har operation naya object deta hai.

    Kaise kaam karta hai — internal representation (PEP 393)¶

    Python 3.3 se CPython flexible string representation use karta hai: string ke content ke hisaab se per-character memory choose hota hai.

    Sab characters Storage Bytes per char
    U+0000 – U+00FF (Latin-1) 1-byte (UCS1) 1
    U+0100 – U+FFFF (BMP) 2-byte (UCS2) 2
    U+10000+ (emoji, rare scripts) 4-byte (UCS4) 4 
    import sys
print(sys.getsizeof(""))            # 49  -- header
print(sys.getsizeof("a"))           # 50  -- +1 byte
print(sys.getsizeof("abc"))         # 52  -- +3 bytes (ASCII -> 1 byte each)
print(sys.getsizeof("é"))           # 74  -- Latin-1 par header bada (ASCII flag off)
print(sys.getsizeof("अ"))           # 78  -- 2-byte storage
print(sys.getsizeof("😀"))          # 80  -- 4-byte storage
    1. Ye per-string decide hota hai, per-character nahi. Ek hi emoji poori string ko 4-byte storage par push kar deta hai.
    2. Faayda: ASCII strings (jo 99% code mein hoti hain) memory-efficient hain aur indexing O(1) rehti hai (fixed width, koi UTF-8 variable-length scanning nahi).
    3. Ye trade-off Python ne deliberately liya: UTF-8 storage memory bachaata par s[i] O(n) ban jaata. Python ne O(1) indexing chuni.

    Kyu += loop mein quadratic hai¶

    lines = ""
for i in range(5):
    lines += f"line {i}\n"

    Har iteration mein kya hota hai:

    i=0: new_str(len 7)   <- allocate 7,  copy 0 + 7   = 7 bytes copied
i=1: new_str(len 14)  <- allocate 14, copy 7 + 7   = 14 bytes copied
i=2: new_str(len 21)  <- allocate 21, copy 14 + 7  = 21 bytes copied
i=3: new_str(len 28)  <- allocate 28, copy 21 + 7  = 28 bytes copied
i=4: new_str(len 35)  <- allocate 35, copy 28 + 7  = 35 bytes copied

Total copied = 7 + 14 + 21 + 28 + 35 = 105 bytes for a 35-byte result

    n iterations ke liye total copy = 7 * (1 + 2 + ... + n) = O(n²).

    Proof¶

    import timeit

def concat_plus(n):
    s = ""
    for i in range(n):
        s += "x" * 10                  # har baar naya string
    return s

def concat_join(n):
    parts = []                         # list mein collect karo -- O(1) amortised append
    for i in range(n):
        parts.append("x" * 10)
    return "".join(parts)              # ek hi allocation, ek hi pass

for n in (1_000, 10_000, 50_000):
    t1 = timeit.timeit(lambda: concat_plus(n), number=5)
    t2 = timeit.timeit(lambda: concat_join(n), number=5)
    print(f"n={n:<7} +=: {t1:.4f}s   join: {t2:.4f}s   ratio: {t1/t2:.1f}x")

    Typical output:

    n=1000    +=: 0.0015s   join: 0.0008s   ratio: 1.9x
n=10000   +=: 0.0180s   join: 0.0075s   ratio: 2.4x
n=50000   +=: 0.2100s   join: 0.0380s   ratio: 5.5x

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. s += "x" * 10 — "x" * 10 compile time par fold ho jaata hai (constant), toh sirf concatenation ka cost hai. Har iteration ek naya object banata hai aur poora purana content copy karta hai.
    2. parts.append(...) — list append amortised O(1) hai (3.1). n appends = O(n).
    3. "".join(parts) — join do pass karta hai: pehle total length compute karta hai (saare parts ka len jodta hai), phir ek allocation karke sab copy karta hai. Total O(total_length). Ye poori technique ka core hai.
    4. Ratio n ke saath badhta hai — ye quadratic vs linear ka signature hai. Agar ye constant factor hota toh ratio same rehta.

    Ek important nuance: CPython mein str.__iadd__ ke liye ek optimization hai — agar string ka refcount 1 hai (matlab sirf yahi ek naam laga hai) toh CPython usko in-place resize karne ki koshish karta hai (unicode_concatenate fast path). Isliye chhote loops mein aapko quadratic behaviour nahi dikhega. Par:

    • Ye optimization guaranteed nahi hai (PyPy, Jython mein nahi hai),
    • Refcount 1 na ho (list mein bhi wahi string ho, ya function argument ho) toh nahi lagti,
    • s = s + x (augmented nahi) par bilkul nahi lagti.

    Isliye hamesha join likho — wo har implementation par linear hai.

    String building ke saare tareeke¶

    rows = [("test_login", "passed", 1.2), ("test_cart", "failed", 4.5)]

# 1. join + comprehension -- default choice
report = "\n".join(f"{name:<15} {status:<8} {dur:.2f}s" for name, status, dur in rows)
print(report)

# 2. join + list -- jab logic complex ho
parts = []
for name, status, dur in rows:
    parts.append(f"{name:<15} {status:<8} {dur:.2f}s")
    if status == "failed":
        parts.append(f"{'':<15} ^^^ see screenshot")
report = "\n".join(parts)

# 3. io.StringIO -- file-like interface, incremental writes
import io
buf = io.StringIO()
buf.write("TEST REPORT\n")
for name, status, dur in rows:
    buf.write(f"{name}: {status} ({dur}s)\n")
report = buf.getvalue()
print(report)

# 4. Textwrap for formatting
import textwrap
print(textwrap.dedent("""\
    TEST REPORT
    -----------
    Total: 2
""").strip())

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. "\n".join(genexp) — generator expression ko join accept karta hai, par internally wo pehle list bana leta hai (kyunki do-pass algorithm ko length pata honi chahiye). Toh yahan laziness ka memory faayda nahi milta — par code saaf hai.
    2. f"{name:<15} {status:<8} {dur:.2f}s" — column alignment. QA reports ke liye ye padhne mein bahut farak daalta hai.
    3. io.StringIO() — in-memory text buffer jo file jaisa interface deta hai. Ye tab useful hai jab wahi code kabhi file mein aur kabhi memory mein likhna ho — ya jab aap print(file=buf) use karna chaho. Internally wo bhi list of chunks rakhta hai.
    4. textwrap.dedent — triple-quoted string ka common leading whitespace hataata hai, taaki aap indented code mein readable template likh sako. """\ mein backslash pehli newline ko nigal jaata hai.

    String slicing aur indexing¶

    s = "test_login_chromium"

print(s[0])                 # 't'      -- O(1)
print(s[-1])                # 'm'      -- last char
print(s[5:10])              # 'login'  -- O(k), naya string
print(s[:4])                # 'test'
print(s[11:])               # 'chromium'
print(s[::-1])              # reversed -- 'muimorhc_nigol_tset'
print(s[::2])               # har doosra char
print(len(s))               # 19       -- O(1), field mein stored

# Slicing NEVER raises IndexError
print(s[100:200])           # ''       -- khaali string, koi error nahi
# print(s[100])             # IndexError: string index out of range
    1. Indexing O(1) hai kyunki fixed-width storage hai (PEP 393).
    2. Slicing O(k) hai jahan k slice ki length hai — naya object banta hai, copy hoti hai. Isliye loop mein baar-baar slice karna costly hai.
    3. s[::-1] reversal ka idiom hai. Ye "".join(reversed(s)) se tez hai.
    4. Slicing out-of-range par error nahi deta, indexing deta hai. Ye asymmetry aksar bugs chhupa deti hai: aap parts = line.split(":") karke parts[1] lete ho aur IndexError milta hai; par line[10:] chupchaap khaali string deta hai.

    Encoding ka basic (Part 11 mein detail)¶

    s = "café"
b = s.encode("utf-8")            # str -> bytes
print(b)                          # b'caf\xc3\xa9'
print(len(s), len(b))            # 4 5   <- chars 4, bytes 5

back = b.decode("utf-8")         # bytes -> str
print(back == s)                 # True

# Galat encoding se mojibake
print(b.decode("latin-1"))       # 'cafÃ©'   -- galat, par ERROR nahi -- silent corruption
    1. encode str → bytes, decode bytes → str. Yaad rakhne ka tareeka: "encode karke wire par bhejo, decode karke padho".
    2. len(s) != len(b) — characters aur bytes alag cheez hain. Non-ASCII ke saath ye farak dikhta hai. Ye tab bug banta hai jab aap DB column width (bytes) aur input validation (characters) ko mix kar dete ho.
    3. b.decode("latin-1") — Latin-1 har byte ko ek character maan leta hai, toh kabhi fail nahi hota aur silently galat text deta hai. Ye "mojibake" ka main source hai. Isliye encoding explicitly likho aur consistent rakho.

    Gotchas¶

    Gotcha 1 — strip character set hai, substring nahi. (1.8 mein dekha)

    Gotcha 2 — split() bina argument alag hai.

    s = "  a   b  \n c  "
print(s.split())              # ['a', 'b', 'c']    -- koi arg nahi: whitespace runs collapse
print(s.split(" "))           # ['', '', 'a', '', '', 'b', '', '\n', 'c', '', '']
print("a,,b".split(","))      # ['a', '', 'b']     -- empty field preserve hota hai
    1. split() (no arg) whitespace ke consecutive runs ko ek separator maanta hai aur leading/ trailing whitespace ignore karta hai — log parsing ke liye yahi chahiye.
    2. split(" ") har single space par todta hai — CSV-jaisa data ke liye yahi chahiye (empty fields matter karte hain).
    3. Ye ek deliberate design hai aur interview mein poochha jaata hai.

    Gotcha 3 — in substring check hai, character nahi.

    print("log" in "test_login")     # True   -- substring
print("gol" in "test_login")     # False  -- order matter karta hai

    Gotcha 4 — string comparison lexicographic hai, natural nahi.

    files = ["test_10.py", "test_2.py", "test_1.py"]
print(sorted(files))                    # ['test_1.py', 'test_10.py', 'test_2.py']  <- "galat"

import re
def natural_key(s):
    """String ko (text, number, text, number...) tuple mein todo."""
    return [int(part) if part.isdigit() else part.lower()
            for part in re.split(r"(\d+)", s)]

print(sorted(files, key=natural_key))   # ['test_1.py', 'test_2.py', 'test_10.py']
    1. String comparison character-by-character code point se hoti hai: "1" < "2" toh "test_10" "test_2" se pehle aata hai.
    2. re.split(r"(\d+)", s) — capturing group hone se separators bhi result mein aate hain: "test_10.py" → ['test_', '10', '.py'].
    3. int(part) if part.isdigit() else part.lower() — numbers ko int banao (numeric comparison), text ko lowercase (case-insensitive).
    4. Result ek list hai jo tuple ki tarah element-wise compare hoti hai. Ye "natural sort" ka standard implementation hai — test file ordering, screenshot ordering mein kaam aata hai.
    5. Caveat: agar ek string mein number ho aur doosri mein us position par text, toh int < str comparison TypeError dega. Robust version mein sab ko (0, int_val) / (1, str_val) tuples mein wrap karo.

    Gotcha 5 — multiline strings mein indentation.

    def get_query():
    return """
    SELECT * FROM tests
    WHERE status = 'failed'
    """                                # ismein leading spaces aur newlines hain!

print(repr(get_query()))
# '\n    SELECT * FROM tests\n    WHERE status = \'failed\'\n    '

import textwrap
def get_query_clean():
    return textwrap.dedent("""\
        SELECT * FROM tests
        WHERE status = 'failed'
    """).strip()

print(repr(get_query_clean()))
# "SELECT * FROM tests\nWHERE status = 'failed'"

    Interview answer: "Strings are immutable sequences of Unicode code points, and since PEP 393 CPython picks the narrowest storage that fits — one, two, or four bytes per character — so ASCII strings stay compact while indexing remains O(1). The consequence of immutability that matters most is that s += x in a loop is quadratic: each concatenation allocates a new string and copies everything so far, so n appends copy O(n squared) bytes. The fix is to collect the pieces in a list and call ''.join(parts) once — join does two passes, summing the lengths and then doing a single allocation, which is linear. CPython does have a fast path that resizes in place when the refcount is one, so small loops don't show the problem, but that's an implementation detail and it disappears the moment a second reference exists, so I write join unconditionally. For incremental building with a file-like interface I use io.StringIO."

    Cross-question — "Why doesn't Python just store strings as UTF-8 internally, like Rust and Go do?" "Because UTF-8 is variable-width, so s[i] would be O(n) — you'd have to scan from the start counting code points. Python's string API promises O(1) indexing and slicing, and a huge amount of existing code relies on that. PEP 393's answer was to pick a fixed width per string based on its widest character, which keeps indexing O(1) while making ASCII strings — the overwhelming majority — one byte per character. Rust and Go went the other way: they store UTF-8 and simply don't offer O(1) character indexing; Rust's String won't let you index by character at all. It's a genuine trade-off, not one language being wrong. CPython does cache the UTF-8 encoding of a string after the first encode('utf-8'), so repeated encoding is cheap."

    3.6 The collections module — poora¶

    collections mein wo containers hain jo built-ins ke gaps bharte hain. QA automation mein inka istemaal roz padta hai.

    3.6.1 defaultdict¶

    Kya hai: ek dict jo missing key par KeyError ki jagah ek factory call karke default value bana deti hai.

    Kyu hai:

    results = [
    {"name": "test_a", "status": "failed"},
    {"name": "test_b", "status": "passed"},
    {"name": "test_c", "status": "failed"},
]

# --- WITHOUT defaultdict: har jagah "key hai kya" check ---
grouped = {}
for r in results:
    if r["status"] not in grouped:            # extra check har item par
        grouped[r["status"]] = []             # manual initialisation
    grouped[r["status"]].append(r["name"])

# --- setdefault se thoda better, par abhi bhi awkward ---
grouped = {}
for r in results:
    grouped.setdefault(r["status"], []).append(r["name"])

# --- WITH defaultdict ---
from collections import defaultdict
grouped = defaultdict(list)                   # missing key -> list() call hoga
for r in results:
    grouped[r["status"]].append(r["name"])    # bas. Koi check nahi.
print(dict(grouped))    # {'failed': ['test_a', 'test_c'], 'passed': ['test_b']}

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. defaultdict(list) — argument ek callable hai, ek value nahi. list (class object) pass kiya, list() nahi. Agar aap defaultdict([]) likho toh TypeError: first argument must be callable or None — kyunki ek hi list share ho jaati aur wo 1.4 wala bug hota. Ye design deliberately safe hai.
    2. grouped[r["status"]] — missing key par __missing__ chalta hai, jo list() call karke naya khaali list banata hai, use dict mein daalta hai, aur return karta hai. Isliye .append seedha kaam kar jaata hai.
    3. dict(grouped) — print karne ke liye plain dict mein badla, kyunki defaultdict ka repr defaultdict(<class 'list'>, {...}) hota hai jo log mein noisy hai.

    Kaise kaam karta hai: defaultdict dict ko subclass karta hai aur __missing__ method define karta hai. dict.__getitem__ jab key na mile toh __missing__ dhoondhta hai — agar mile toh use call karta hai, warna KeyError.

    Common factories:

    from collections import defaultdict

counts = defaultdict(int)                # missing -> 0
counts["failed"] += 1                    # 0 + 1
print(dict(counts))                      # {'failed': 1}

lists = defaultdict(list)                # missing -> []
sets = defaultdict(set)                  # missing -> set()
nested = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(list))    # nested grouping
nested["chromium"]["failed"].append("test_a")
print(nested["chromium"]["failed"])      # ['test_a']

# Custom default
def default_result():
    return {"passed": 0, "failed": 0}
stats = defaultdict(default_result)
stats["chromium"]["passed"] += 1
print(dict(stats))                       # {'chromium': {'passed': 1, 'failed': 0}}
    1. defaultdict(int) — int() 0 deta hai. Counting ke liye — par Counter isse behtar hai.
    2. defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(list)) — nested. Lambda isliye ki har baar naya defaultdict bane. Note: ye pickle nahi ho sakta (lambda picklable nahi hai) — agar aapko multiprocessing mein bhejna ho toh module-level function use karo.
    3. defaultdict(default_result) — apna factory. Named function lambda se behtar hai jab logic ho, aur wo picklable bhi hai.

    Gotcha — read karne se bhi key ban jaati hai:

    d = defaultdict(list)
print(len(d))              # 0
if d["missing_key"]:       # sirf CHECK kar rahe the...
    pass
print(len(d))              # 1   <- key ban gayi!
print(dict(d))             # {'missing_key': []}
    1. d["missing_key"] __getitem__ hai, jo __missing__ call karke key insert kar deta hai. Ye "read-only" nahi hai.
    2. Ye bug tab dikhta hai jab aap baad mein len(d) ya d.keys() par bharosa karte ho — aapke grouping mein khaali groups aa jaate hain.
    3. Fix: check karne ke liye if "missing_key" in d: ya d.get("missing_key") use karo — dono __missing__ trigger nahi karte.

    Interview answer: "defaultdict takes a zero-argument factory and calls it when a key is missing, via the __missing__ hook that dict.__getitem__ looks for. It removes the if key not in d: d[key] = [] boilerplate from every grouping loop. The argument is a callable, not a value — defaultdict(list), not defaultdict([]) — which is deliberate, because a shared mutable default would be the classic aliasing bug. The gotcha is that reading a missing key inserts it, so if d[k]: mutates the dict; I use k in d or d.get(k) when I only want to look."

    Cross-question — "When would you use setdefault instead of defaultdict?" "When only some of the accesses should create a default, or when I need a plain dict at the end. defaultdict changes the behaviour of every lookup on the object forever, including lookups elsewhere in the code that just meant to check. setdefault is per-call and explicit. The cost is that setdefault's default is evaluated eagerly on every call even when the key exists — d.setdefault(k, expensive()) always calls expensive() — so for expensive defaults defaultdict or an explicit if wins. In practice I use defaultdict inside a local accumulation loop and convert with dict(...) before returning it, so callers get normal KeyError behaviour."

    3.6.2 Counter¶

    Kya hai: ek dict subclass jo elements ko count karta hai.

    from collections import Counter

statuses = ["passed", "failed", "passed", "skipped", "passed", "failed"]

c = Counter(statuses)
print(c)                          # Counter({'passed': 3, 'failed': 2, 'skipped': 1})
print(c["passed"])                # 3
print(c["nonexistent"])           # 0    <- KeyError NAHI, zero
print(c.most_common(2))           # [('passed', 3), ('failed', 2)]
print(c.total())                  # 6    (Python 3.10+)
print(sum(c.values()))            # 6    (har version)
print(list(c.elements()))         # ['passed','passed','passed','failed','failed','skipped']

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. Counter(statuses) — iterable se counts. Ye C level par optimised hai (_count_elements), manual loop se ~2x tez.
    2. c["nonexistent"] → 0 — Counter.__missing__ 0 deta hai aur key insert nahi karta (ye defaultdict se alag aur behtar hai).
    3. c.most_common(2) — top-2, count descending. Ties ka order insertion order hai (3.7+). Argument na do toh sab, sorted.
    4. c.total() — 3.10+. Purane versions mein sum(c.values()).
    5. c.elements() — counts ko wapas flat iterator mein badalta hai. Zero ya negative counts skip hote hain.

    Counter arithmetic — ye asli power hai:

    from collections import Counter

run1 = Counter({"passed": 40, "failed": 5, "skipped": 2})
run2 = Counter({"passed": 38, "failed": 8, "skipped": 1})

print(run2 - run1)              # Counter({'failed': 3})  -- sirf POSITIVE bachta hai
print(run1 - run2)              # Counter({'passed': 2, 'skipped': 1})
print(run1 + run2)              # sab jod do
print(run1 & run2)              # min of each -- Counter({'passed': 38, 'failed': 5, ...})
print(run1 | run2)              # max of each

# Negative bhi chahiye toh subtract() use karo (in-place)
diff = Counter(run2)
diff.subtract(run1)
print(diff)                     # Counter({'failed': 3, 'skipped': -1, 'passed': -2})
    1. run2 - run1 — subtraction sirf positive counts rakhta hai (multiset semantics). Isliye "kaun se failures badhe" ye ek line hai.
    2. subtract() — in-place, aur negative counts rakhta hai. Regression detection ke liye ye chahiye: -2 passed matlab do tests jo pehle pass ho rahe the ab nahi.
    3. & aur | multiset intersection/union hain (min aur max counts).

    QA use cases:

    from collections import Counter
import re

# 1. Error types ki frequency log se
log = """
ERROR TimeoutError: locator not found
ERROR AssertionError: expected 200 got 500
ERROR TimeoutError: locator not found
ERROR ConnectionError: refused
ERROR TimeoutError: page load
"""
error_types = Counter(re.findall(r"ERROR (\w+):", log))
print(error_types.most_common())    # [('TimeoutError', 3), ('AssertionError', 1), ...]

# 2. Duplicate test names dhoondho
names = ["test_a", "test_b", "test_a", "test_c", "test_b", "test_a"]
dupes = {name: n for name, n in Counter(names).items() if n > 1}
print(dupes)                        # {'test_a': 3, 'test_b': 2}

# 3. Do lists ko multiset ki tarah compare karo (order ignore, duplicates count)
expected = ["a", "b", "b", "c"]
actual = ["b", "a", "c", "b"]
print(Counter(expected) == Counter(actual))    # True -- same elements, same counts
print(set(expected) == set(actual))            # True bhi -- par duplicates ignore karke
    1. re.findall(r"ERROR (\w+):", log) — capturing group hone se findall sirf group deta hai, poori match nahi. Directly Counter mein ja sakta hai.
    2. {name: n for name, n in Counter(names).items() if n > 1} — duplicates nikalne ka one-liner. Ye pytest collection mein duplicate test IDs pakadne ke liye seedha useful hai.
    3. Counter(expected) == Counter(actual) — multiset equality. Ye sorted(a) == sorted(b) se tez hai (O(n) vs O(n log n)) aur set(a) == set(b) se correct hai, kyunki wo duplicates ignore kar deta hai. Test assertions mein "same items, order doesn't matter, but duplicates matter" ke liye yahi sahi hai.

    Gotcha:

    c = Counter("hello")
print(c)                    # Counter({'l': 2, 'h': 1, 'e': 1, 'o': 1})
# String iterate hoti hai character-by-character -- shayad ye aap nahi chahte the

c = Counter(["hello"])      # list mein daalo agar poora word count karna hai
print(c)                    # Counter({'hello': 1})

c = Counter(a=3, b=1)       # kwargs se bhi
c.update(["a", "c"])        # ADD karta hai, replace nahi
print(c)                    # Counter({'a': 4, 'b': 1, 'c': 1})

    Interview answer: "Counter is a dict subclass for multisets. Missing keys return zero without inserting, which makes counting loops clean, and most_common(n) gives the top-n directly. What I actually use is its arithmetic: run2 - run1 on two counters of test statuses gives the counts that increased, and subtract keeps the negatives so I can see regressions. Counter(a) == Counter(b) is my go-to for order-insensitive list comparison in assertions — unlike set(a) == set(b) it respects duplicates, and unlike sorted(a) == sorted(b) it's O(n) and doesn't require the elements to be orderable."

    Cross-question — "How is Counter different from defaultdict(int)?" "Both give you zero for a missing key, but defaultdict(int) inserts the key when you read it while Counter doesn't — so a Counter you only read from stays clean. Beyond that, Counter adds most_common, elements, total, and the multiset operators + - & |, plus an update that adds rather than overwrites. And its constructor counts an iterable directly in C, which is roughly twice as fast as a Python loop incrementing a defaultdict. The one thing defaultdict(int) does better is being a plain accumulator when the values aren't really counts — Counter with negative or float values works but the multiset operations start behaving oddly."

    3.6.3 deque — double-ended queue¶

    Kya hai: deque ("deck") ek doubly-linked list of fixed-size blocks hai. Dono ends par O(1) append/pop.

    Kyu hai:

    # --- list ko queue ki tarah use karna: O(n) per pop ---
queue = ["task1", "task2", "task3"]
next_task = queue.pop(0)              # O(n) -- saare elements shift

# --- deque: O(1) ---
from collections import deque
queue = deque(["task1", "task2", "task3"])
next_task = queue.popleft()           # O(1) -- bas pointer badla

    import timeit

t_list = timeit.timeit("q.pop(0)", setup="q = list(range(100000))", number=100_000)
t_deque = timeit.timeit("q.popleft()", setup="from collections import deque; q = deque(range(100000))", number=100_000)
print(f"list.pop(0):    {t_list:.4f}s")     # ~1.5s
print(f"deque.popleft(): {t_deque:.4f}s")   # ~0.005s  -- 300x tez

    Kaise kaam karta hai: internally deque blocks ka doubly-linked list hai (har block mein 64 pointers). Left ya right par add karne ke liye sirf block ka pointer badalta hai — koi shifting nahi. Trade-off: middle mein index access O(n) hai (blocks traverse karne padte hain), jabki list mein O(1).

    Poori API:

    from collections import deque

d = deque(["a", "b", "c"])

# --- Both ends ---
d.append("d")                # O(1) right
d.appendleft("z")            # O(1) left
print(d)                     # deque(['z', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd'])
print(d.pop())               # O(1) 'd'
print(d.popleft())           # O(1) 'z'

d.extend(["x", "y"])         # O(k) right
d.extendleft(["p", "q"])     # O(k) left -- NOTE: order ULTA aata hai!
print(d)                     # deque(['q', 'p', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'x', 'y'])

# --- Rotation ---
d = deque([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
d.rotate(2)                  # right rotate: last 2 aage aa gaye
print(d)                     # deque([4, 5, 1, 2, 3])
d.rotate(-2)                 # left rotate: wapas
print(d)                     # deque([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

# --- BOUNDED deque -- ye sabse useful feature hai ---
recent = deque(maxlen=3)     # sirf aakhri 3 rakho
for i in range(6):
    recent.append(i)
print(recent)                # deque([3, 4, 5], maxlen=3)   -- purane apne aap gir gaye

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. d.extendleft(["p", "q"]) — har item ek-ek karke left par append hota hai, toh p pehle left par aaya, phir q uske left par → final order q, p. Ye reversal expected behaviour hai aur documented hai, par surprise deta hai.
    2. d.rotate(2) — O(k) hai jahan k rotation ki magnitude hai. Round-robin scheduling ke liye useful.
    3. deque(maxlen=3) — bounded deque. maxlen par pahunchne ke baad ek taraf se add karne par doosri taraf se automatically discard hota hai. Ye ek fixed-size sliding window free mein deta hai.

    QA use cases:

    from collections import deque

# 1. Last-N log lines rakhna (crash ke waqt context ke liye)
class LogTail:
    def __init__(self, n=50):
        self._lines = deque(maxlen=n)          # sirf aakhri n, memory bounded

    def write(self, line):
        self._lines.append(line)               # O(1), purane apne aap gir jaate hain

    def dump(self):
        return "\n".join(self._lines)

tail = LogTail(n=3)
for i in range(10):
    tail.write(f"line {i}")
print(tail.dump())                             # sirf line 7, 8, 9

# 2. BFS -- page graph crawl karna
def crawl(start, get_links, max_pages=100):
    seen = {start}                             # set: O(1) membership
    queue = deque([start])                     # BFS ke liye FIFO
    order = []
    while queue and len(order) < max_pages:
        url = queue.popleft()                  # O(1) -- yahi jagah list slow hoti
        order.append(url)
        for link in get_links(url):
            if link not in seen:               # O(1) set lookup
                seen.add(link)
                queue.append(link)             # O(1)
    return order

# 3. Sliding window -- last 5 test durations ka average
window = deque(maxlen=5)
for d in [1.2, 3.4, 0.8, 2.1, 5.0, 1.1, 0.9]:
    window.append(d)
    print(f"rolling avg: {sum(window) / len(window):.2f}")

    Line-by-line walkthrough (BFS):

    1. seen = {start} — set literal. Membership O(1). Agar list use karte toh har check O(n) aur poora crawl O(n²).
    2. queue = deque([start]) — BFS ko FIFO chahiye. popleft O(1) hai. list.pop(0) se ye O(n²) ho jaata.
    3. while queue and len(order) < max_pages: — queue truthy hai jab tak khaali na ho. and short-circuit karta hai, toh khaali queue par len(order) check nahi hota.
    4. if link not in seen: — seen mein add karo enqueue karte waqt, dequeue karte waqt nahi. Warna ek hi URL multiple baar queue mein aa jaayega (duplicate work).
    5. Ye exactly wo algorithm hai jo ek site crawler ya "saare links check karo ki 404 toh nahi" test likhne mein use hota hai.

    Gotchas:

    from collections import deque
d = deque([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
print(d[0])              # 1   -- O(1), ends ke paas
print(d[2])              # 3   -- O(n), beech mein traverse
# d[1:3]                 # TypeError: sequence index must be integer -- SLICING NAHI!
import itertools
print(list(itertools.islice(d, 1, 3)))    # [2, 3]   -- islice se karo
    1. Deque slicing support nahi karta. Ye deliberate hai — slicing O(n) hoti aur log usko O(1) samajh lete.
    2. Middle indexing O(n) hai. Agar aapko random access chahiye toh list use karo.
    3. sort() bhi nahi hai — sorted(d) naya list dega.

    Interview answer: "deque is a doubly-linked list of fixed-size blocks, so appends and pops at both ends are O(1), unlike a list where pop(0) and insert(0, x) are O(n) because every remaining pointer shifts. That makes it the right structure for queues and for BFS — in a link crawler, using a list as the queue turns the whole crawl quadratic. The feature I use most is maxlen: a bounded deque automatically discards from the other end, which gives me a fixed memory sliding window for free — I keep the last fifty log lines for crash context and the last N durations for a rolling average, with no manual trimming. The trade-off is that indexing into the middle is O(n) and slicing isn't supported at all, so for random access a list is still correct."

    3.6.4 namedtuple¶

    Kya hai: ek factory jo tuple subclass banati hai jismein fields ke naam hote hain.

    Kyu hai:

    # --- Plain tuple: magic indices ---
result = ("test_login", "passed", 1.2, "chromium")
if result[1] == "passed":                  # [1] kya hai? Code padhne wale ko nahi pata
    print(result[0], "took", result[2])    # aur agar field add ho jaaye toh sab shift

# --- Dict: better, par typo-prone aur bhaari ---
result = {"name": "test_login", "status": "passed", "duration": 1.2}
if result["staus"] == "passed":            # TYPO -> KeyError at runtime, sirf us branch mein

# --- namedtuple: naam bhi, tuple ke saare faayde bhi ---
from collections import namedtuple
TestResult = namedtuple("TestResult", ["name", "status", "duration", "browser"])
result = TestResult("test_login", "passed", 1.2, "chromium")
if result.status == "passed":              # padhne mein saaf
    print(result.name, "took", result.duration)

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. namedtuple("TestResult", [...]) — pehla argument class ka naam hai (string), jo repr aur pickling mein use hota hai. Isko left side wale variable jaisa hi rakho, warna repr confusing hoga aur pickle tootega.
    2. Fields list, ya space/comma separated string bhi de sakte ho: namedtuple("TestResult", "name status duration browser").
    3. TestResult(...) — ye ek class hai, toh instantiate karo. Ye internally ek real class generate karta hai (source code likhkar exec se!) jo tuple se inherit karti hai.
    4. result.status — attribute access. Internally ye property hai jo _tuple_getitem(1) karta hai — toh runtime cost lagbhag zero hai.

    Poori API:

    from collections import namedtuple

TestResult = namedtuple("TestResult", "name status duration browser")

r = TestResult("test_login", "passed", 1.2, "chromium")

# --- Access ---
print(r.name)                    # attribute se
print(r[0])                      # index se bhi -- ye tuple hai
name, status, dur, browser = r   # unpacking bhi

# --- Tuple ke saare guna ---
print(len(r))                    # 4
print(r == ("test_login", "passed", 1.2, "chromium"))   # True -- plain tuple ke barabar!
print(hash(r) == hash(("test_login", "passed", 1.2, "chromium")))   # True

# --- namedtuple ke apne methods (underscore se, taaki field naam se clash na ho) ---
print(r._asdict())               # {'name': 'test_login', 'status': 'passed', ...}
r2 = r._replace(status="failed") # NAYA object (immutable hai!)
print(r2.status, r.status)       # failed passed
print(TestResult._fields)        # ('name', 'status', 'duration', 'browser')
print(TestResult._make(["test_x", "passed", 0.5, "firefox"]))   # iterable se banao

# --- Defaults (Python 3.7+) ---
TestResult2 = namedtuple("TestResult2", "name status duration browser",
                         defaults=("passed", 0.0, "chromium"))   # RIGHTMOST fields ko
print(TestResult2("test_a"))     # TestResult2(name='test_a', status='passed', ...)

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. r == ("test_login", ...) → True — namedtuple ek tuple hai, toh plain tuple se equal ho sakta hai. Ye faayda bhi hai (existing tuple-based code se compatible) aur khatra bhi (do alag namedtuple types jinke values same hain wo bhi equal honge — Point(1,2) == Color(1,2) True hai!).
    2. _asdict() — dict deta hai. JSON serialization ke liye: json.dumps(r._asdict()).
    3. _replace(status="failed") — immutable hai, toh "modify" ka matlab naya object banana hai. Ye functional-style update hai. r.status = "failed" AttributeError dega.
    4. _fields — field names ka tuple. Generic code likhne ke liye (CSV header banana, etc.).
    5. _make(iterable) — CSV row se banane ke liye: TestResult._make(csv_row).
    6. Underscore prefix kyun? Kyunki user ke field names kuch bhi ho sakte hain. asdict naam ka field ho sakta hai, toh method ka naam _asdict rakha gaya taaki clash na ho. Ye "private" nahi hai — ye public API hai jise deliberately underscore diya gaya.
    7. defaults=(...) — rightmost fields ko apply hote hain, exactly function defaults ki tarah. Toh defaults=("passed",) sirf browser ko default dega, status ko nahi.

    Typed version — typing.NamedTuple (better)

    from typing import NamedTuple

class TestResult(NamedTuple):
    name: str
    status: str = "passed"                # default
    duration: float = 0.0
    browser: str = "chromium"

    @property
    def is_slow(self) -> bool:            # methods bhi add kar sakte ho!
        return self.duration > 3.0

    def summary(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name}: {self.status} ({self.duration:.2f}s)"

r = TestResult("test_login", "failed", 4.5)
print(r.is_slow)                          # True
print(r.summary())                        # test_login: failed (4.50s)
print(r._asdict())                        # sab kuch abhi bhi kaam karta hai

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. class TestResult(NamedTuple): — ye class syntax hai par internally wahi namedtuple banta hai. Ye modern default hai — type hints milte hain (mypy check kar sakta hai), methods add kar sakte ho, aur padhne mein saaf hai.
    2. name: str — annotation. Runtime par ye enforce nahi hota, sirf mypy/pyright check karte hain. TestResult(123) runtime par chalega.
    3. status: str = "passed" — default. Defaults ke baad koi non-default field nahi aa sakta — bilkul function parameters ki tarah.
    4. @property def is_slow — computed field. Ye tuple mein store nahi hota, har baar compute hota hai. Isliye len(r) abhi bhi 4 hai.
    5. Ye pattern QA mein bahut fit karta hai: immutable test result records jo compare, hash, aur sort ho sakte hain.

    Kab namedtuple vs dataclass vs dict

    Chahiye Use
    Immutable record, tuple compatibility, hashable, unpacking NamedTuple
    Mutable record, methods, inheritance, __post_init__ @dataclass
    Immutable record + validation + no tuple behaviour @dataclass(frozen=True)
    Dynamic keys jo runtime par decide hoti hain dict
    JSON se aaya hua data with known shape TypedDict ya pydantic

    Gotchas:

    from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple("Point", "x y")
Color = namedtuple("Color", "x y")
print(Point(1, 2) == Color(1, 2))         # True !!  -- dono tuples hain
print(Point(1, 2) == (1, 2))              # True

# Field naam Python keyword nahi ho sakta
# Bad = namedtuple("Bad", "class def")    # ValueError: Type names and field names cannot be a keyword
Ok = namedtuple("Ok", "class_ def_", rename=False)   # underscore lagao
Auto = namedtuple("Auto", ["class", "1bad"], rename=True)  # rename=True -> _0, _1
print(Auto._fields)                        # ('_0', '_1')
    1. Type-safety nahi hai — do alag namedtuples equal ho sakte hain. Agar ye matter karta hai toh @dataclass(frozen=True) use karo, jo type bhi compare karta hai.
    2. rename=True invalid names ko _0, _1 bana deta hai — CSV headers se dynamic namedtuple banane ke liye useful.

    Interview answer: "namedtuple generates a tuple subclass with named fields, so you get result.status instead of result[1] while keeping everything a tuple gives you — immutability, hashability, unpacking, and O(1) attribute access because the fields compile down to index lookups. I use typing.NamedTuple with class syntax rather than the functional form, because it gives me annotations mypy can check and lets me add properties and methods. _replace gives me a modified copy since the object is immutable, and _asdict makes JSON serialisation trivial. The trap is that it is a tuple, so two different namedtuple types with the same values compare equal, and so does a plain tuple — if type identity matters I use a frozen dataclass instead."

    3.6.5 OrderedDict¶

    Kya hai: ek dict subclass jo insertion order explicitly maintain karta hai aur order ko semantics ka hissa maanta hai.

    Kyu — 3.7 ke baad bhi kyun exist karta hai

    Plain dict 3.7+ mein ordered hai, par teen cheezein OrderedDict hi deta hai:

    from collections import OrderedDict

# 1. ORDER-SENSITIVE EQUALITY
d1 = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
d2 = {"b": 2, "a": 1}
print(d1 == d2)                                        # True  -- order ignore

od1 = OrderedDict([("a", 1), ("b", 2)])
od2 = OrderedDict([("b", 2), ("a", 1)])
print(od1 == od2)                                      # False -- order matters
print(od1 == d1)                                       # True  -- dict se compare mein order ignore
