    tuple/frozenset instead of list/set ~30% 3.2
    String join instead of += O(n) vs O(n^2) 3.5
    Streaming file reads Poori file → chunk 11.1

    Interview answer: "CPython uses reference counting as the primary mechanism — every object has a counter, and it is freed the instant it hits zero, which is why deterministic cleanup works. Reference cycles defeat that, so there's a second, generational cycle collector: it only tracks containers, keeps three generations on the assumption that most objects die young, and detects unreachable cycles by subtracting internal references from the refcounts.

    weakref is what I use to hold a reference without keeping the object alive — a WeakSet of event listeners means a reporter can be garbage collected even though the bus still nominally knows about it, which is a classic long-running-suite leak.

    When a suite grows in memory over hours, my process is: take an object census with gc.get_objects() every fifty tests and diff the type counts, find which type is growing, then use gc.get_referrers to see what's holding it. In test frameworks the usual suspects are lru_cache on a method — because self becomes part of the cache key so every instance stays alive forever — storing exception objects, since their traceback pins every frame and its locals, and browser contexts or generator fixtures that are never closed. For the last one I store traceback.format_exc() as a string instead of the exception object, which releases the frames immediately. tracemalloc gives me the allocation site with a snapshot diff, and I wire it into an opt-in autouse fixture that fails any test leaking more than a threshold."

    Part 15 — Testing in Python¶

    15.1 unittest vs pytest¶

    # --- unittest: xUnit style, class-based ---
import unittest


class TestLogin(unittest.TestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        cls.browser = "shared per class"

    def setUp(self):
        self.page = "fresh per test"

    def test_valid_login(self):
        result = {"status": "passed", "code": 200}
        self.assertEqual(result["status"], "passed")
        self.assertIn("code", result)
        self.assertTrue(result["code"] == 200)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(1.0, 1.0000001, places=5)
        with self.assertRaises(KeyError):
            result["missing"]

    def tearDown(self):
        pass


# --- pytest: plain functions, plain assert ---
import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def page():
    return "fresh per test"


def test_valid_login(page):
    result = {"status": "passed", "code": 200}
    assert result["status"] == "passed"
    assert "code" in result
    assert result["code"] == 200
    assert result["code"] == pytest.approx(200)
    with pytest.raises(KeyError):
        result["missing"]
    unittest pytest
    Style Classes, self.assertX Functions, plain assert
    Assertion messages Manual ya method-specific Auto-rewritten, detailed
    Setup/teardown setUp/tearDown Fixtures (composable, scoped)
    Parametrisation subTest (limited) @parametrize (first-class)
    Plugins Kam 1000+
    Stdlib Haan Nahi (pip install)
    Runs unittest tests — Haan

    pytest jeetta hai, par unittest jaanna zaruri hai — legacy suites aur unittest.mock (jo pytest bhi use karta hai).

    15.2 Assertion rewriting¶

    def test_comparison():
    result = {"name": "test_login", "status": "failed", "duration": 4.5}
    expected = {"name": "test_login", "status": "passed", "duration": 4.5}
    assert result == expected

    Output:

    E       AssertionError: assert {'duration': 4.5, 'name': 'test_login', 'status': 'failed'} ==
E                              {'duration': 4.5, 'name': 'test_login', 'status': 'passed'}
E         Common items: {'duration': 4.5, 'name': 'test_login'}
E         Differing items: {'status': 'failed'} != {'status': 'passed'}

    Kaise: pytest test modules ko import karte waqt unka AST rewrite karta hai. Har assert expr ko ek expanded version se replace kar deta hai jo sub-expressions ki values capture karta hai. Isliye plain assert se rich output milta hai.

    Isliye:

    1. conftest.py aur test modules mein assertion rewriting automatic hai.
    2. Helper modules mein nahi — unke liye pytest.register_assert_rewrite("mypackage.helpers") conftest.py mein likhna padta hai.
    3. python -O (optimised mode) assert statements ko hata deta hai — toh production code mein assert validation ke liye kabhi mat use karo.

    15.3 Fixtures¶

    import pytest


# --- Basic ---
@pytest.fixture
def config() -> dict:
    return {"env": "staging", "timeout": 30_000}


# --- Yield fixture: setup + teardown ---
@pytest.fixture
def browser_page(browser):
    context = browser.new_context()                # SETUP
    page = context.new_page()
    yield page                                     # test ko diya
    context.close()                                # TEARDOWN


# --- Scopes ---
@pytest.fixture(scope="function")   # default -- har test
def per_test(): ...

@pytest.fixture(scope="class")      # har test class
def per_class(): ...

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")     # har module
def per_module(): ...

@pytest.fixture(scope="package")    # har package
def per_package(): ...

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")    # poore run mein ek baar (PER WORKER xdist mein!)
def per_session(): ...


# --- Autouse: bina maange lag jaati hai ---
@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def reset_state():
    yield
    clear_caches()


# --- Parametrised fixture: har param par test dobara chalta hai ---
@pytest.fixture(params=["chromium", "firefox", "webkit"])
def browser_name(request) -> str:
    return request.param


# --- Factory fixture: test ko parameters dene do ---
@pytest.fixture
def make_user():
    created = []

    def _make(role: str = "customer", **overrides):
        user = {"email": f"{role}@test.com", "role": role, **overrides}
        created.append(user)
        return user

    yield _make
    for u in created:                              # teardown: sab cleanup
        delete_user(u)


def test_admin_can_delete(make_user):
    admin = make_user(role="admin")
    victim = make_user(role="customer")
    assert admin["role"] == "admin"


# --- request object ---
@pytest.fixture
def artifact_path(request, tmp_path):
    return tmp_path / f"{request.node.name}.png"


# --- Dynamic fixture lookup ---
@pytest.fixture
def client(request):
    if request.node.get_closest_marker("live"):
        return request.getfixturevalue("live_client")
    return request.getfixturevalue("mock_client")


def clear_caches(): ...
def delete_user(u): ...

    Key points:

    1. yield fixture — setup, yield, teardown. Teardown reverse dependency order mein chalti hai (7.3).
    2. Scope trade-off: session-scoped fixtures tez hain par state leak ka khatra hai. Ek test ne browser context ka cookie set kiya toh agla test use dekhega.
    3. autouse=True — har test par. Sparingly use karo — hidden dependencies banata hai.
    4. params=[...] — fixture parametrisation. Har dependent test har param ke liye dobara chalta hai — exponential growth ka dhyaan rakho.
    5. Factory fixture — sabse powerful pattern. Test ko control deta hai aur cleanup automatic rehti hai.
    6. request.getfixturevalue(name) — runtime par fixture resolve karo.

    15.4 conftest.py resolution order¶

    tests/
  conftest.py                <- SAARE tests ko dikhta hai
  ui/
    conftest.py              <- sirf tests/ui/** ko
    test_login.py
  api/
    conftest.py              <- sirf tests/api/** ko
    test_orders.py

Resolution: test file se UPAR ki taraf chalte jao, rootdir tak.
Nearest definition WINS (override).

tests/ui/test_login.py ke liye order:
  1. tests/ui/conftest.py       <- highest priority
  2. tests/conftest.py
  3. rootdir/conftest.py
  4. Installed plugins
  5. Built-in fixtures

    # tests/conftest.py
import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def base_url() -> str:
    return "https://staging.example.com"


# tests/ui/conftest.py -- OVERRIDE
import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def base_url(base_url) -> str:                     # parent fixture ko REQUEST kar sakte ho!
    return base_url + "/app"                       # aur extend

    conftest.py ke rules:

    1. Import karne ki zarurat nahi — pytest automatically discover karta hai.
    2. Hooks (pytest_configure, pytest_collection_modifyitems) sirf conftest.py ya plugins mein.
    3. Rootdir ke bahar wale conftest.py load nahi hote.
    4. Same naam ki fixture override karne par aap parent version ko argument ki tarah maang sakte ho — ye extension ka clean pattern hai.

    15.5 Parametrisation¶

    import pytest


# --- Basic ---
@pytest.mark.parametrize("status_code,expected", [
    (200, "success"),
    (301, "redirect"),
    (404, "client-error"),
    (500, "server-error"),
])
def test_classify(status_code, expected):
    assert classify(status_code) == expected


# --- Custom IDs ---
@pytest.mark.parametrize("email,valid", [
    pytest.param("a@b.com", True, id="simple"),
    pytest.param("a+tag@b.co.in", True, id="plus-and-subdomain"),
    pytest.param("no-at-sign", False, id="missing-at"),
    pytest.param("", False, id="empty", marks=pytest.mark.xfail(reason="BUG-123")),
])
def test_email_validation(email, valid):
    assert is_valid_email(email) is valid


# --- Stacked: CARTESIAN PRODUCT ---
@pytest.mark.parametrize("browser", ["chromium", "firefox"])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("viewport", ["desktop", "mobile"])
def test_renders(browser, viewport):
    ...                                            # 2 x 2 = 4 tests


# --- Indirect: fixture ko parametrise karo ---
@pytest.fixture
def user(request):
    role = request.param
    return {"role": role, "email": f"{role}@test.com"}


@pytest.mark.parametrize("user", ["admin", "customer"], indirect=True)
def test_permissions(user):
    assert user["role"] in ("admin", "customer")


# --- Dynamic generation ---
def pytest_generate_tests(metafunc):
    """Hook: runtime par parameters generate karo."""
    if "browser" in metafunc.fixturenames:
        browsers = metafunc.config.getoption("--browsers", default="chromium").split(",")
        metafunc.parametrize("browser", browsers)


def classify(code): return "success"
def is_valid_email(e): return "@" in e

    Key points:

    1. pytest.param(..., id="...") — readable test IDs. Bina iske test_email_validation[a+tag@b.co.in-True] dikhta hai.
    2. marks=pytest.mark.xfail(...) — per-parameter marks. Ek known-broken case ko xfail karo bina poora test skip kiye.
    3. Stacked parametrize — cartesian product. Exponential — 3 stacked decorators with 3 values each = 27 tests.
    4. indirect=True — parameter fixture ko jaata hai, test ko nahi. Complex setup ke liye.
    5. pytest_generate_tests — CLI options se parametrisation. --browsers=chromium,firefox.

    15.6 Markers¶

    import pytest


# pyproject.toml mein register karo (--strict-markers ke saath MANDATORY)
# markers = ["smoke: quick sanity", "slow: >30s", "flaky: intermittent"]

@pytest.mark.smoke
def test_homepage_loads(): ...

@pytest.mark.slow
@pytest.mark.parametrize("n", [1, 2])
def test_bulk_import(n): ...

@pytest.mark.skip(reason="feature not implemented yet")
def test_future_feature(): ...

@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.version_info < (3, 11), reason="needs 3.11 TaskGroup")
def test_taskgroup(): ...

@pytest.mark.xfail(reason="BUG-1234", strict=True)
def test_known_broken(): ...                       # PASS ho jaaye toh suite FAIL (strict)

@pytest.mark.timeout(30)                            # pytest-timeout plugin
def test_bounded(): ...

pytestmark = pytest.mark.integration                # MODULE-level: har test par lagta hai


# Programmatic marking
def pytest_collection_modifyitems(config, items):
    """Path ke hisaab se automatically mark karo."""
    for item in items:
        if "slow" in item.nodeid or "e2e" in item.nodeid:
            item.add_marker(pytest.mark.slow)
        if "integration" in str(item.fspath):
            item.add_marker(pytest.mark.integration)

    pytest -m smoke                            # sirf smoke
pytest -m "not slow"                       # slow chhod ke
pytest -m "smoke and not flaky"            # boolean expressions
pytest -k "login and not logout"           # NAAM se filter (-k, marker nahi)

    --strict-markers zaruri hai — bina uske @pytest.mark.smok (typo) silently ignore hota hai aur wo test kabhi filter mein nahi aayega.

    15.7 Mocking — where to patch (recap + practice)¶

    (Poora treatment 12.9 mein.) Ek line ka rule: patch where it's looked up, not where it's defined.

    # myapp/service.py
#     from myapp.api import fetch_status          <- naya binding bana
#
# GALAT: patch("myapp.api.fetch_status")
# SAHI:  patch("myapp.service.fetch_status")

    import pytest
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock


# --- pytest ka monkeypatch fixture -- automatic undo ---
def test_env_dependent(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("TEST_ENV", "prod")
    monkeypatch.delenv("DEBUG", raising=False)
    monkeypatch.setattr("myapp.config.TIMEOUT", 1000)
    monkeypatch.setitem(some_dict, "key", "value")
    monkeypatch.chdir("/tmp")
    # Sab automatically undo -- test ke baad

    monkeypatch patch se better hai pytest mein: automatic cleanup, aur env vars/dict items ke liye dedicated methods.

    15.8 Coverage¶

    pip install pytest-cov
pytest --cov=src/qa_framework --cov-report=term-missing --cov-report=html --cov-branch

    [tool.coverage.run]
source = ["src/qa_framework"]
branch = true                          # BRANCH coverage -- line se better
omit = ["*/tests/*", "*/__main__.py"]

[tool.coverage.report]
show_missing = true
fail_under = 80
exclude_lines = [
    "pragma: no cover",
    "if TYPE_CHECKING:",
    "raise NotImplementedError",
    "if __name__ == .__main__.:",
    "@abstractmethod",
]

    Line vs branch coverage:

    def check(x):
    if x > 0:
        return "positive"
    return "other"

# test_check(): check(1)
# LINE coverage: 100% (dono lines chalein? nahi -- 'return "other"' nahi chali)
# Actually: line coverage 75%, branch coverage 50%
# 'if' ka False branch kabhi test nahi hua

    Coverage ke limits:

    1. Coverage correctness nahi batati — 100% coverage wala code galat ho sakta hai. Wo sirf "ye line chali" batata hai, "ye line sahi hai" nahi.
    2. Assertion-less tests bhi coverage dete hain — def test_x(): my_function() 100% coverage de sakta hai bina kuch verify kiye.
    3. Mutation testing (mutmut, cosmic-ray) actual test quality measure karta hai — wo code mein bugs inject karke dekhta hai ki tests pakadte hain ya nahi.

    15.9 Property-based testing with Hypothesis¶

    # pip install hypothesis
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st, settings, assume, example, HealthCheck


@given(st.text())
def test_normalise_is_idempotent(s: str):
    """Kisi bhi string par: normalise(normalise(x)) == normalise(x)"""
    once = normalise(s)
    assert normalise(once) == once


@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
def test_sort_properties(lst: list[int]):
    result = sorted(lst)
    assert len(result) == len(lst)                 # length preserve
    assert all(a <= b for a, b in zip(result, result[1:]))    # ordered
    assert sorted(result) == result                # idempotent
    from collections import Counter
    assert Counter(result) == Counter(lst)         # same elements


@given(
    email=st.emails(),
    age=st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=150),
    tags=st.lists(st.text(min_size=1), max_size=5, unique=True),
)
@settings(max_examples=200, deadline=1000, suppress_health_check=[HealthCheck.too_slow])
@example(email="a@b.co", age=0, tags=[])           # ye case HAMESHA test hoga
def test_user_serialisation(email, age, tags):
    user = {"email": email, "age": age, "tags": tags}
    import json
    assert json.loads(json.dumps(user)) == user


@given(st.floats(allow_nan=False, allow_infinity=False, min_value=0))
def test_duration_formatting(seconds: float):
    assume(seconds < 1e6)                          # unrealistic values skip karo
    result = format_duration(seconds)
    assert isinstance(result, str)
    assert len(result) > 0


# --- Stateful testing ---
from hypothesis.stateful import RuleBasedStateMachine, rule, invariant


class CartStateMachine(RuleBasedStateMachine):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.items: list[dict] = []

    @rule(name=st.text(min_size=1), price=st.floats(min_value=0.01, max_value=10000))
    def add_item(self, name, price):
        self.items.append({"name": name, "price": price})

    @rule()
    def remove_last(self):
        if self.items:
            self.items.pop()

    @invariant()
    def total_is_non_negative(self):
        assert sum(i["price"] for i in self.items) >= 0

    @invariant()
    def count_matches(self):
        assert len(self.items) >= 0


TestCart = CartStateMachine.TestCase


def normalise(s): return " ".join(s.split()).lower()
def format_duration(s): return f"{s:.2f}s"

    Line-by-line walkthrough:

    1. @given(st.text()) — Hypothesis hundreds of inputs generate karta hai, including edge cases: khaali string, unicode, surrogates, very long strings.
    2. Properties, examples nahi: aap "ye input → ye output" nahi likhte; aap "har input ke liye ye sach hona chahiye" likhte ho.
    3. Shrinking — failure milne par Hypothesis minimal failing case dhoondhta hai. Ek 500 character wali string se "\x00" tak shrink kar deta hai.
    4. @example(...) — specific case jo hamesha test ho (known regression).
    5. assume(condition) — us input ko skip karo (retry ke saath).
    6. @settings(deadline=1000) — per-example timeout. Browser tests ke liye badhana padta hai.
    7. RuleBasedStateMachine — sequences of operations generate karta hai aur invariants check karta hai. Ye QA ke liye bahut powerful hai — cart, session, ya state machine testing.

    Kab useful: parsers, serialisers, validators, normalisers, calculations, state machines. Kab nahi: UI flows, integration tests jahan har run costly ho.

    Interview answer: "pytest wins over unittest for three reasons: plain assert with AST-level rewriting that gives you a diff instead of 'assertion failed'; fixtures, which compose and have scopes rather than a single setUp; and first-class parametrisation. Fixtures resolve by walking up from the test file through each conftest.py to the rootdir, with the nearest definition winning — and an overriding fixture can request the parent version by name, which is how I extend a base URL per directory rather than duplicating it.

    The pattern I use most is the factory fixture: instead of returning a fixed object, it returns a function the test calls with its own parameters, while the fixture records what was created and cleans it up in the teardown after the yield. That gives per-test control with automatic cleanup. On scopes, session-scoped fixtures are the performance lever and the flakiness risk — and under xdist they run once per worker, not once per run.

    On mocking, the rule is patch where the name is looked up, not where it's defined, and always autospec=True so a signature change breaks the test instead of silently passing. And I treat coverage as a floor, not a goal — a test with no assertions still produces coverage, so I use branch coverage and, where the logic is worth it, Hypothesis: I state a property like 'normalise is idempotent' and it generates hundreds of inputs and shrinks any failure to a minimal reproducer."

    Part 16 — Idioms and Code Quality¶

    16.1 EAFP vs LBYL¶

    Kya hai¶

    Do styles hain kisi risky operation ko handle karne ke:

    • LBYL — Look Before You Leap. Pehle check karo, phir karo. (if key in d: d[key])
    • EAFP — Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission. Kar do, exception pakad lo.

    Python EAFP prefer karta hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    Do reasons: (1) race condition — check aur use ke beech mein duniya badal sakti hai (file delete ho gayi, key dusre thread ne pop kar di); (2) speed — happy path par try ka cost ~0 hai, jabki if har baar chalta hai.

    import os, json

# --- LBYL: race condition ka darwaza khula hai ---
def load_config_lbyl(path):
    if os.path.exists(path):                  # check -- is instant par file thi
        # <-- yahan doosra process file delete kar sakta hai (TOCTOU bug)
        with open(path) as f:                 # use  -- yahan tak me gayab ho sakti hai
            return json.load(f)
    return {}                                 # silent default

# --- EAFP: atomic, no gap ---
def load_config_eafp(path):
    try:
        with open(path) as f:                 # seedha try karo -- open() khud atomic hai
            return json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:                 # sirf yahi expected failure pakdo
        return {}                             # baaki (PermissionError, JSONDecodeError) upar jaayein

# --- QA example: report parser ---
def duration_of(test_case: dict) -> float:
    try:
        return float(test_case["time"])       # 99% cases: key hai aur numeric hai
    except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError): # missing / None / "N/A" -- teeno ek jagah
        return 0.0

    Kab LBYL sahi hai: jab exception normal ho (loop mein 50% keys missing) — tab dict.get() ya in faster aur saaf hai. EAFP tab jeetta hai jab failure rare ho.

    Gotcha¶

    try block ko chhota rakho, warna galat line ka exception pakad loge:

    d = {"a": {"b": 1}}
try:
    value = d["a"]["c"]        # 'c' missing -- KeyError
except KeyError:
    value = None               # aapko laga 'a' missing tha, actually 'c' tha
print(value)                   # None  -- bug chhup gaya, debugging mein 1 ghanta gaya

    16.2 Idiom cheat table¶

    Non-Pythonic Pythonic Kyu
    for i in range(len(xs)): xs[i] for x in xs: index ki zarurat hi nahi
    for i in range(len(xs)): i, xs[i] for i, x in enumerate(xs): ek hi pass, no manual counter
    for i in range(len(a)): a[i], b[i] for x, y in zip(a, b): length mismatch par chhota jeetega
    tmp = a; a = b; b = tmp a, b = b, a tuple packing, atomic
    if len(xs) > 0: if xs: truthiness protocol
    if x == None: if x is None: identity, __eq__ override-proof
    s = "" + loop s += p "".join(parts) O(n) vs O(n^2)
    d[k] if k in d else v d.get(k, v) ek lookup
    if k not in d: d[k] = [] d.setdefault(k, []) / defaultdict atomic
    "Hi " + name + "!" f"Hi {name}!" fast + readable
    os.path.join(a, b) Path(a) / b typed, cross-platform
    type(x) == list isinstance(x, list) subclass-safe
    lambda x: x[1] for sort operator.itemgetter(1) C-level, faster
    manual flag loop any(...) / all(...) short-circuits 
    from operator import itemgetter

results = [                                    # pytest report se aaya hua data
    {"name": "test_login", "ms": 4200, "status": "passed"},
    {"name": "test_cart",  "ms":  180, "status": "failed"},
    {"name": "test_pay",   "ms": 9100, "status": "passed"},
]

slowest = max(results, key=itemgetter("ms"))               # C-level key, lambda se tez
any_failed = any(r["status"] == "failed" for r in results) # genexp -- pehle fail par ruk jaata hai
slow_names = [r["name"] for r in results if r["ms"] > 1000]# filter + map ek hi comprehension mein
report = "\n".join(f"{i}. {n}" for i, n in enumerate(slow_names, start=1))  # start=1 -- human numbering

print(slowest["name"], any_failed, report, sep=" | ")
# test_pay | True | 1. test_login
# 2. test_pay

    16.3 PEP 8, naming, aur tooling¶

    Kya hai¶

    PEP 8 = style guide. Black = opinionated formatter (bahas khatam). Ruff = linter (+ formatter), flake8/isort/pyupgrade ka fast replacement. Mypy = static type checker.

    Cheez Convention Example
    module / package lower_snake page_objects.py
    function / variable lower_snake wait_for_toast()
    class CapWords CheckoutPage
    constant UPPER_SNAKE DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 30
    "internal" _leading_underscore _driver
    name-mangled __two_underscores __cache (class-private)
    keyword clash trailing_ class_, id_ 
    # pyproject.toml -- ek hi jagah poora quality setup
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100                  # black default 88; team ne 100 chuna
target-version = "py311"           # is version ke liye rewrites suggest karo

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "SIM", "PT"]
# E/F = pycodestyle+pyflakes, I = import sort, UP = pyupgrade,
# B = bugbear (mutable default arg pakadta hai), SIM = simplify, PT = pytest style

[tool.mypy]
strict = true                      # sab strict flags on
disallow_untyped_defs = true       # bina annotation wala def error
warn_unused_ignores = true         # purane '# type: ignore' hatao

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "-ra --strict-markers"   # strict-markers = typo'd marker error dega

    # .pre-commit-config.yaml -- commit par khud chalega, CI se pehle
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    rev: v0.6.9
    hooks:
      - id: ruff                   # lint, --fix ke saath
        args: [--fix]
      - id: ruff-format            # formatting

    Gotcha¶

    Type hints runtime par enforce nahi hote — sirf mypy check karta hai:

    def timeout(seconds: int) -> str:
    return seconds * 2             # int lauta raha hai, hint kehta hai str

print(timeout("ab"))               # abab   -- koi error nahi! Python ne hint ignore kiya
print(timeout.__annotations__)     # {'seconds': <class 'int'>, 'return': <class 'str'>}

    Interview answer: "Pythonic code is about using the language's protocols instead of reimplementing them. Concretely: iterate over objects rather than indices, use enumerate and zip instead of manual counters, lean on truthiness rather than len(x) > 0, use is None for identity, and join strings rather than building them with += in a loop — that last one is O(n^2) because strings are immutable.

    On error handling I default to EAFP over LBYL. Checking os.path.exists before opening is a TOCTOU race — the file can disappear between the check and the open — and on the happy path a try block costs essentially nothing while an if runs every iteration. The discipline is to keep the try body to the one line that can fail and catch the narrowest exception, or you end up swallowing a different bug.

    For quality I don't argue about style: Black or ruff-format settles formatting, ruff handles linting and import ordering, mypy in strict mode catches type errors, and pre-commit runs all three before the commit lands so CI is a safety net, not the first feedback. One thing I'm explicit about with the team is that type hints are not enforced at runtime — they're documentation plus a static check, so validation at trust boundaries still needs real code."

    Part 17 — Interview Closing¶

    17.1 Forty rapid-fire questions¶

    Ye wo sawaal hain jinka jawab do line mein, bina soche aana chahiye. Left column padho, jawab bol kar bolo, phir right column se milao.

    # Question Short English answer
    1 Is Python interpreted or compiled? Both — source compiles to bytecode, then the CPython VM interprets that bytecode.
    2 is vs ==? is compares identity (same object in memory), == compares value via __eq__.
    3 What is the GIL? A mutex letting only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so threads don't parallelise CPU work — I/O still overlaps because the GIL is released during blocking calls.
    4 List vs tuple? List is mutable and unhashable; tuple is immutable, hashable if its contents are, and slightly smaller and faster.
    5 Shallow vs deep copy? Shallow copies the outer container and shares the nested objects; copy.deepcopy recursively duplicates everything.
    6 Why is the mutable default argument a bug? Defaults are evaluated once at function-definition time, so one list is shared by every call. Use None and create inside.
    7 What does __init__ do — is it the constructor? No, __new__ allocates the object; __init__ only initialises the already-created instance.
    8 Explain MRO. The linearised order Python searches for attributes, computed with C3 linearisation; super() walks that order, not "the parent".
    9 @staticmethod vs @classmethod? staticmethod gets no implicit first argument; classmethod receives the class, so it respects subclassing — that's why it's used for alternative constructors.
    10 What is a generator? A function with yield that returns a lazy iterator, producing values one at a time and keeping its local state between resumes.
    11 Generator vs list comprehension? The list builds everything in memory immediately; the generator expression is lazy, O(1) memory, and single-pass.
    12 What is a decorator? A callable that takes a function and returns a replacement — @d is just f = d(f).
    13 Why functools.wraps? Without it the wrapper replaces __name__, __doc__ and __wrapped__, which breaks introspection, docs and pytest's fixture discovery.
    14 What is a closure? A nested function that keeps a reference to a variable from its enclosing scope, stored in __closure__ cells.
    15 Explain LEGB. Name resolution order: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in.
    16 global vs nonlocal? global rebinds a module-level name; nonlocal rebinds the nearest enclosing function's name.
    17 What makes an object iterable vs an iterator? Iterable defines __iter__; an iterator defines both __iter__ and __next__ and is consumed once.
    18 How does with work? The context manager's __enter__ runs on entry and __exit__ always runs on exit, including on exception; returning True from __exit__ suppresses it.
    19 try/except/else/finally order? try runs, except on a match, else only if no exception, finally always — and a return in finally overrides everything.
    20 Why is bare except: bad? It also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. Use except Exception at minimum, and the narrowest type you can.
    21 raise X from Y? Explicit exception chaining — sets __cause__ so the traceback shows the original root cause.
    22 Dict lookup complexity? Amortised O(1) via hashing; worst case O(n) on pathological collisions.
    23 What makes an object hashable? It implements __hash__ and __eq__ and its hash never changes — so mutable built-ins like list and dict are unhashable.
    24 Are dicts ordered? Yes — insertion-ordered since 3.7 as a language guarantee (3.6 as an implementation detail).
    25 __str__ vs __repr__? __str__ is for users, __repr__ for developers and should be unambiguous; repr is the fallback when str is missing.
    26 What is __slots__ for? It replaces the per-instance __dict__ with fixed descriptors, cutting memory and speeding attribute access, at the cost of dynamic attributes.
    27 How does CPython manage memory? Reference counting as the primary mechanism, plus a generational cycle collector to free reference cycles.
    28 When would you use weakref? For caches and back-references that must not keep the target alive — a weak reference doesn't raise the refcount.
    29 Threading vs multiprocessing vs asyncio? Threads for blocking I/O, processes for CPU-bound work (separate interpreters, no shared GIL), asyncio for high-concurrency I/O in one thread with explicit await points.
    30 What does await actually do? Suspends the coroutine and yields control to the event loop until the awaited awaitable completes.
    31 *args and **kwargs? Collect extra positional args into a tuple and extra keyword args into a dict; at the call site the same syntax unpacks.
    32 What does / and * mean in a signature? Everything before / is positional-only, everything after * is keyword-only.
    33 Are type hints enforced? No — they're ignored at runtime; only a static checker like mypy validates them.
    34 __init__.py — what is it for? It marks a regular package and runs on import; without it you get an implicit namespace package.
    35 Why a virtual environment? Per-project isolated dependency versions, so projects don't fight over one global site-packages.
    36 Where do you patch when mocking? Where the name is looked up, not where it's defined — and with autospec=True so signature changes fail the test.
    37 Mock vs MagicMock? MagicMock additionally pre-configures the dunder protocols, so it supports len(), iteration, context managers and comparisons.
    38 Fixture scopes in pytest? function, class, module, package, session — and under xdist a session fixture runs once per worker, not once per run.
    39 Is 100% coverage a good goal? No — a test with no assertions still produces coverage. It's a floor for finding untested code, not a proof of correctness.
    40 Name three things that make code Pythonic. Iterating over objects instead of indices, EAFP over LBYL, and using protocols (truthiness, context managers, iterators) instead of reimplementing them.

    17.2 Fifteen output-prediction puzzles¶

    Rule: pehle output likho, phir reasoning padho. Jo galat nikle wahi aapka revision list hai.

    1. Mutable default

    def collect(item, acc=[]):     # acc ka default list EK BAAR bana, def ke waqt
    acc.append(item)           # har call usi shared list ko modify karta hai
    return acc

r1 = collect("test_login")     # ['test_login']
r2 = collect("test_cart")      # ['test_login', 'test_cart']
print(r1, r2)
    Output: ['test_login', 'test_cart'] ['test_login', 'test_cart'] Reasoning: default def execute hote waqt evaluate hota hai, call par nahi. r1 aur r2 ek hi object ke naam hain — isliye dono same dikhte hain. Fix: acc=None + acc = acc or [].

    2. Late binding closure

    fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]   # teeno lambda 'i' ko dekhte hain, uski VALUE ko nahi
print([f() for f in fns])             # call ab ho raha hai, jab loop khatam ho chuka
    Output: [2, 2, 2] Reasoning: closure variable ko by reference capture karta hai. Call ke waqt i ki last value 2 hai. Fix: lambda i=i: i — default arg definition-time par freeze kar deta hai.

    3. bool is int

    d = {True: 'a', 1: 'b', 1.0: 'c'}   # True == 1 == 1.0, aur hash bhi same
print(d)
    Output: {True: 'c'} Reasoning: dict keys equality se dedupe hoti hain. Teeno equal hain, isliye ek hi entry — key pehli wali (True) rehti hai, value aakhri wali ('c') overwrite ho jaati hai.

    4. Tuple + +=

    t = ([1],)          # tuple immutable, par uske andar ka list mutable
t[0] += [2]         # ye do kaam karta hai: list.__iadd__ (success) phir t[0] = ... (fail)
    Output: TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment — par t ab ([1, 2],) hai. Reasoning: += list par in-place extend karta hai (mutation ho gayi), phir result ko wapas t[0] par assign karne ki koshish karta hai — wahan tuple mana kar deta hai. Half-done state.

    5. Generator exhaustion

    g = (i for i in range(4))   # lazy iterator, ek hi baar chalega
print(sum(g), sum(g))       # pehla sum poora consume kar leta hai
    Output: 6 0 Reasoning: generator single-pass hai. Doosre sum() ko khaali iterator mila, aur khaali sum 0 hota hai — koi error nahi. QA mein ye bug fixtures se generator return karne par milta hai.

    6. finally swallows return

    def h():
    try:
        return "try"        # ye value hold ho jaati hai...
    finally:
        return "finally"    # ...par finally ka return use overwrite kar deta hai
print(h())
    Output: finally Reasoning: finally hamesha chalta hai aur agar usme return/break ho toh wo pending return aur pending exception dono ko discard kar deta hai. Isliye finally mein return mat likho.

    7. List multiplication aliasing

    grid = [[0] * 3] * 3    # bahar wala * inner list ka REFERENCE 3 baar copy karta hai
grid[0][0] = 9          # ek row badli...
print(grid)
    Output: [[9, 0, 0], [9, 0, 0], [9, 0, 0]] Reasoning: teeno rows ek hi list object hain. Fix: [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)] — comprehension har iteration mein nayi list banati hai.

    8. Float equality

    print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)   # binary floating point exact nahi hai
print(0.1 + 0.2)
    Output: False aur 0.30000000000000004 Reasoning: 0.1 aur 0.2 binary mein exactly represent nahi hote (IEEE-754). Fix: math.isclose(a, b) ya pytest.approx, aur paise ke liye decimal.Decimal.

    9. Chained comparison

    print(1 in [1, 2] == True)   # ye chain hai, left-to-right nahi
    Output: False Reasoning: Python isko (1 in [1, 2]) and ([1, 2] == True) mein expand karta hai. Pehla True hai, doosra False — isliye False. Comparison operators chain hote hain.

    10. Mutating while iterating

    xs = [1, 2, 3, 4]
for x in xs:            # iterator index 0,1,2... track kar raha hai
    if x % 2 == 0:
        xs.remove(x)    # list chhoti ho gayi, index aage badh gaya -> ek element skip
print(xs)
    Output: [1, 3] Reasoning: 2 remove hone par 3 index 1 par aa gaya, par iterator index 2 par chala gaya — 3 skip ho gaya... aur 4 fir bhi mila. Fix: xs = [x for x in xs if x % 2] ya copy par iterate.

    11. Class attribute shared

    class Suite:
    tags = []                        # CLASS attribute -- sab instances mein ek hi
    def add(self, t):
        self.tags.append(t)          # append MUTATE karta hai, rebind nahi -> class wali badli

a, b = Suite(), Suite()
a.add("smoke")
print(b.tags)
    Output: ['smoke'] Reasoning: self.tags.append ne lookup class par kiya aur usi list ko mutate kiya. Agar self.tags = [...] likhte toh instance attribute banta aur class wali safe rehti. Fix: __init__ mein self.tags = [].

    12. UnboundLocalError

    timeout = 10
def run():
    print(timeout)      # yahan hi error -- pehle line par
    timeout = 5         # ye assignment poore function mein 'timeout' ko LOCAL bana deta hai
run()
    Output: UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'timeout' where it is not associated with a value Reasoning: scope compile time par decide hota hai, poore function ke liye. Function mein kahin bhi assignment hai toh naam local hai — global read nahi hoga. Fix: global timeout.

    13. zip truncates

    print(list(zip([1, 2, 3], [4, 5])))   # chhoti sequence jeetati hai
    Output: [(1, 4), (2, 5)] Reasoning: zip silently shortest par ruk jaata hai — 3 chup-chaap gir gaya. QA mein ye data-mismatch bug chhupata hai. Fix: zip(a, b, strict=True) (3.10+) — length mismatch par raise.

    14. Sort stability

    rows = [(1, 'b'), (1, 'a'), (0, 'c')]
print(sorted(rows, key=lambda p: p[0]))   # sirf pehle element par sort
    Output: [(0, 'c'), (1, 'b'), (1, 'a')] Reasoning: Python ka sort stable hai — equal keys wale items apna original relative order rakhte hain, isliye 'b' 'a' se pehle hi raha. Isi wajah se multi-key sort ke liye aap kam-important key par pehle sort kar sakte ho.

    15. Truthiness aur out-of-range slice

    print(bool([]), bool([[]]), bool("0"))   # khaali vs "khaali list wali list" vs string "0"
print([1, 2, 3][10:])                    # slice range se bahar
    Output: False True True aur [] Reasoning: [[]] mein ek element hai isliye truthy; "0" non-empty string hai isliye truthy (sirf "" falsy hai). Slicing out-of-range par exception nahi deta — khaali list deta hai, jabki indexing ([10]) IndexError deta.

    17.3 Mistakes that cost offers¶

    Galti Kyu bura lagta hai Iske badle bolo
    "Python is interpreted" full stop Adhoora jawab, bytecode ka pata nahi lagta "Compiled to bytecode, then interpreted by the CPython VM"
    "GIL means Python can't do concurrency" Threads vs parallelism ka confusion "The GIL blocks CPU parallelism in threads; I/O still overlaps, and processes bypass it"
    except Exception: pass code sample mein Production instinct kharab dikhta hai Narrow exception + log + re-raise ya explicit fallback
    Har jagah time.sleep() Flaky automation ka red flag Explicit waits / polling with timeout
    "I'd write a loop" har question ka jawab Idioms nahi pata enumerate, zip, comprehension, any/all naam lo
    Whiteboard par super(MyClass, self) Python 2 ki aadat Zero-arg super()
    "Deep copy is safer, I always use it" Cost ka andaza nahi "Shallow by default; deepcopy only when nested state is shared"
    Coverage number ko quality bolna Metric gaming "Coverage is a floor; assertions and branch coverage are the signal"
    Mock ko patch('module_where_defined') karna Common real bug "Patch where the name is looked up"
    Type hints ko runtime validation bolna Basic misconception "Hints are static-only; validate at trust boundaries"

    17.4 Night-before revision sheet¶

    # --- Ek page mein poora doc ---

# 1. NAMES vs OBJECTS: variable ek name tag hai. '=' rebind karta hai, mutate nahi.
#    Function args pass-by-object-reference: mutable ko mutate kiya toh caller ko dikhega.

# 2. MUTABILITY: list/dict/set mutable; str/tuple/frozenset/int immutable.
#    Mutable default arg = def-time par ek baar bana. None sentinel use karo.

# 3. COMPLEXITY: list index O(1), list `in` O(n), append O(1) amortised, insert(0) O(n).
#    dict/set lookup O(1) avg. String += loop mein O(n^2) -> "".join() use karo.

# 4. LEGB: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. Function mein assignment = local (compile time).
#    global = module-level rebind, nonlocal = enclosing rebind.

# 5. OOP: __new__ allocate, __init__ initialise. MRO = C3 linearisation, super() usi order par
#    chalta hai. @classmethod = alternative constructor. __slots__ = no __dict__, less memory.

# 6. GENERATORS: yield = lazy, single-pass, O(1) memory. yield from delegate karta hai.
#    Generator ko fixture se return kiya toh doosra consumer khaali paayega.

# 7. DECORATOR: @d ka matlab f = d(f). functools.wraps hamesha lagao.
#    Arguments wale decorator = teen level nesting (factory -> decorator -> wrapper).

# 8. CONTEXT MANAGER: __enter__/__exit__; __exit__ True return kare toh exception dab jaata hai.
#    @contextmanager + yield, aur ExitStack dynamic number of resources ke liye.

# 9. EXCEPTIONS: try/except/else/finally. finally mein return = sab kuch nigal jaata hai.
#    'raise X from Y' chaining. Bare except KeyboardInterrupt bhi pakadta hai.

# 10. CONCURRENCY: I/O-bound -> threads ya asyncio. CPU-bound -> processes.
#     GIL sirf bytecode execution par lock hai, blocking I/O ke dauran release ho jaata hai.

# 11. MEMORY: refcount primary + generational GC cycles ke liye. weakref refcount nahi badhata.

# 12. TESTING: fixtures compose hoti hain aur conftest.py se resolve hoti hain (nearest wins).
#     autospec=True, patch where looked up, branch coverage, Hypothesis for properties.

# 13. PYTHONIC: EAFP > LBYL, protocols use karo, truthiness, enumerate/zip, is None.

    Aakhri 30 minute mein sirf ye teen cheez dohrao: mutable default argument, late-binding closure, aur "patch where it's looked up". Ye teeno har Python interview mein aate hain.

    Interview answer: "If I had to compress what I actually rely on day to day: first, Python has names and objects, not boxes — assignment rebinds a name while mutation changes the object every name points at, and almost every surprising bug I've debugged, from the mutable default argument to a shared class attribute, is that one model being applied wrongly.

    Second, most of the language is protocols. Iteration, context management, truthiness, equality and hashing are all just dunder methods, so the idiomatic move is to implement the protocol rather than reimplement the behaviour — that's what makes generators, with, and decorators feel like one coherent system instead of three features.

    Third, for the work I do — test automation — the highest-leverage pieces are generators and context managers for resource lifecycle, decorators for cross-cutting concerns like retry and timing, pytest fixtures for composable setup, and a clear-eyed view of the GIL so I pick threads for I/O-bound browser work and processes for genuinely CPU-bound work. And I hold two habits firmly: catch the narrowest exception I can and never swallow it silently, and let the tooling — ruff, mypy, pre-commit — enforce style so code review can be about design instead."

    End of document. Part 0 se Part 17 tak — ab REPL kholo aur pehla code block type karo.
